(c) except for multi-engine aeroplane operations, select power, attitude and configuration as required for the flight path, balance and trim the aeroplane accurately, and apply smooth, coordinated control inputs to achieve stable flight at the required flight tolerances that apply to the following:

(i) minimum approach speed with flaps retracted;

(ii) minimum approach speed in approach configuration;

(iii) flight at speeds just above stall warning activation or at the initial symptoms of stall;

(d) except for multi-engine aeroplane operations, observe audible and visible stall warnings and recover aeroplane to controlled flight;

(e) recognise and respond positively to reduced effectiveness of controls during slow flight manoeuvres;

(f) recognise the need to increase power while manoeuvring in slow flight to maintain nominated altitude and a margin of speed above the stall;

(g) transition from slow speed configuration, using take‑off power to achieve nominated speed in excess of 1.5 Vs without loss of height.

**A3.6 – Perform circuits and approaches** operate and monitor all aircraft systems when operating the aeroplane in the circuit; in accordance with specific local procedures, safely perform a full circuit pattern (5 legs) by balancing and trimming the aeroplane accurately while applying smooth, coordinated control inputs to achieve the required flight tolerances specified for the flight path flown during traffic pattern manoeuvres as follows: track upwind along extended centreline to 500 ft; establish and maintain cross-wind leg tracking 90° to the runway; establish and maintain downwind leg tracking parallel to, and at a specified distance from, the runway at circuit height; establish base leg tracking 90° to the runway at a specified distance from the runway threshold; perform checks as required throughout circuit; establish the approach and landing configuration appropriate for the runway and meteorological conditions, and adjust the power plant controls as required for the following: commence and control approach descent path; adjust descent commencement point to take account of extended downwind leg or traffic adjustments; align and maintain aircraft on final approach flight path with specified or appropriate runway; set and maintain approach configuration not below 500 ft AGL; identify and maintain the nominated aiming point; maintain a stabilised approach angle at the nominated airspeed not less than 1.3VS to the round-out height; verify existing wind conditions, make proper correction for drift, and maintain a precise ground track; apply speed allowances for wind gusts; configure aeroplane for landing; maintain aircraft separation and position in the circuit with reference to other aircraft traffic in the circuit area.

**A3.7 – Local area airspace** using an appropriate chart, for the local area and circuit area: identify geographical features; identify geographical limits; identify restricted, controlled and uncontrolled airspace areas; state local airspace limits; identify the transit route between the departure aerodrome and training area; identify the geographical limits of the training area; identify aerodromes and landing areas within the local area; maintain orientation and pinpoint location by using geographical features and a local area chart; transit from the circuit area and transit to the designated training area; operate safely within a transit lane (if applicable); remain clear of restricted, controlled and other appropriately designated airspace; operate safely in the vicinity of local aerodromes and landing areas; transit from the designated training area to the circuit area; set QNH appropriately; correctly determine which runway is to be used for landing; ensure runway is serviceable and available; position aircraft for arrival into the circuit.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; aeroplane with piston or turbine powerplant and propeller; aircraft with fixed or retractable undercarriage; aircraft with or without flaps; simulated hazardous weather; approach and landing configurations: normal; flapless; glide; circuit patterns: normal 1,000 ft AGL circuit; low-level 500 ft AGL circuit; full circuit pattern, including 5 legs; shortened circuit pattern; day VFR conditions; local area airspace limitations.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the primary effects of controls; the secondary effects of controls; the stall warning devices; aircraft systems; aircraft performance; aircraft weight and balance; hazards when performing performance manoeuvres; turning using a magnetic compass; relationship between angle of bank, load factor and stall speed; relationship between induced drag and operating at slow speed; dangers associated with mechanical and wake turbulence; engine considerations during prolonged climbing and descending; contents of the aircraft flight manual and pilot’s operating handbook; environmental conditions that represent VMC; day VFR flight rules; local area operating procedures; relevant sections of the AIP.

A4 Land aeroplane

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct a landing in an aeroplane.

Elements and performance criteria **A4.1 – Land aeroplane** maintain a constant landing position aim point; achieve a smooth, positively-controlled transition from final approach to touchdown, including the following; control ballooning during flare; touchdown at a controlled rate of descent, in the specified touchdown zone within tolerances control bouncing after touchdown; touchdown aligned with the centreline within tolerances; ensure separation is maintained; maintain positive directional control and cross-wind correction during the after-landing roll; use drag and braking devices, as applicable, in such a manner to bring the airplane to a safe stop; complete the applicable after-landing checklist items in a timely manner. **A4.2 – Land aeroplane in a cross-wind** verify existing wind conditions, make proper correction for drift, and maintain a precise ground track; configure the aeroplane for the cross-wind conditions; control the aeroplane during the transition from final approach to touchdown and during after-landing roll to compensate for the cross-wind conditions. **A4.3 – Conduct a missed approach** recognise the conditions when a missed approach should be executed; make the decision to execute a missed approach when it is safe to do so; make a smooth, positively-controlled transition from approach to missed approach, including the following: select power, attitude and configuration to safely control aeroplane; manoeuvre aeroplane clear of the ground and conduct after take-off procedures; make allowance for wind velocity during go-around; avoid wake turbulence. **A4.4 – Perform recovery from missed landing** recognise when a missed landing is occurring and when it is appropriate to take recovery action; make the decision to execute recovery from a missed landing only when it is safe to do so; make a smooth, positively-controlled transition from missed landing to missed approach, including the following: select power, attitude and configuration to safely control aeroplane; manoeuvre aeroplane clear of the ground and conduct after take-off procedures; make allowance for wind velocity during go-around; avoid wake turbulence. **A4.5 – Short landing** land aeroplane at nominated touchdown point at minimum speed; control ballooning during flare; control bouncing after touchdown; maintain direction after touchdown; apply maximum braking without locking up wheels; stops aircraft within landing distance available.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; aeroplane with piston or turbine powerplant and propeller; aircraft with nose wheel or tail wheel; aircraft with fixed or retractable undercarriage; aircraft with or without flaps; sealed, gravel or grass runways and taxiways; windsock located on aerodrome; simulated hazardous weather; day VFR conditions; for landing an aeroplane in cross-wind, the cross-wind component must be: for RPL, not more than 10 kts; otherwise, 70% of the maximum permitted for the type of aeroplane being flown; local area operational limitations such as noise abatement and aerodrome curfews.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: typical single-engine aeroplane aircraft systems; aeroplane performance; aeroplane limitations; aeroplane weight and balance; options when local conditions are not suitable for landing; causes of loss of control of aeroplane on landing; contents of the aircraft flight manual and pilot’s operating handbook; environmental conditions that represent VMC; day VFR flight rules; propeller wash, rotor wash and jet blast; relevant sections of the AIP.

A5 Aeroplane advanced manoeuvres

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to perform advanced manoeuvres in an aeroplane.

Elements and performance criteria

2.1 A5.1 – Enter and recover from stall

(a) perform stalling pre-manoeuvre checks;

(b) recognise symptoms of a stall;

(c) control the aeroplane by trimming and balancing accurately for slow flight and then applying the required pitch, roll and yaw inputs to enter and recover from the following:

(i) slow flight where initial symptoms of a stall become evident;

(ii) stall, recovering without application of power;

(iii) stall, recovering with full power applied (not required for multi-engine aeroplanes);

(iv) stall under the following conditions:

(A) straight and level flight;

(B) climbing flight (not required for multi-engine aeroplanes);

(C) descending flight (not required for multi-engine aeroplanes);

(D) approach to land configuration;

(E) turning flight (not required for multi-engine aeroplanes);

(d) perform stall recovery including the following:

(i) reduce angle of attack;

(ii) prevent yaw;

(iii) use available power and height to increase the aircraft energy state;

(iv) avoid secondary stall;

(v) re-establish desired flight path and aircraft control with balanced control application;

(e) perform stall recovery in simulated partial and complete engine failure conditions;

(f) perform stall recovery at simulated low altitude.

2.2 A5.2 – Avoid spin

This element only applies to a single-engine aeroplane:

(a) perform stalling pre-manoeuvre checks;

(b) recognise wing drop at the stall;

(c) from balanced flight, recover from stall in the attitudes and configurations most likely to cause a wing drop;

(d) perform recovery where the aeroplane exhibits a tendency to drop a wing at the stall, in accordance with paragraph (d) of subclause 2.1 (5.1 – Enter and recover from stall);

(e) perform stall recovery at simulated low altitude.

2.3 A5.3 – Turn aeroplane steeply

pre-manoeuvre checks for steep turning;

steep level turn using a nominated bank angle, ending on a nominated heading or geographical feature, without altitude change;

steep descending turn using a nominated bank angle, ending on a nominated heading or geographical feature ending on a nominated altitude;

aeroplane operating limits are not exceeded.

2.4 A5.4 – Sideslip aeroplane (where flight manual permits)

straight sideslip: induce slip to achieve increased rate of descent while maintaining track and airspeed; and adjust rate of descent by coordinating angle of bank and applied rudder;

sideslipping turn by adjusting the bank angle to turn through minimum heading change of 90° at constant airspeed using sideslip, and exiting the turn on a specified heading or geographical feature, within tolerance;

recover from a sideslip and return the aeroplane to balanced flight.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; manoeuvres are performed within operating limits of aeroplane; aeroplane with piston or turbine powerplant and propeller; aircraft with nose wheel or tail wheel; aircraft with fixed or retractable undercarriage; aircraft with or without flaps; sealed, gravel or grass runways and taxiways; windsock located on aerodrome; simulated hazardous weather; day VFR conditions; local area operational limitations such as noise abatement and aerodrome curfews.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: operational circumstances where steep turns are required; aerodynamic and aeroplane operational considerations related to slow flight, sideslipping, stalling, spinning, steep turns, upset aeroplane states, including but not limited to the following: symptoms of approach to stall and throughout the stall manoeuvre until recovery; relationship between angle of attack and stall; effects of weight, centre of gravity position, ‘g’ force and angle of attack; dangers of unbalanced flight; principle of stick and control and the point of stall; priority given to reduce angle of attack during stall manoeuvres; loss of height is considered in relation to available height and energy state; the technique of converting excess speed to height; the technique of converting excess height to speed; symmetrical and rolling ‘g’ force limitations; higher stall speeds when aeroplane is turning; effects on fuel, pitot and flap systems; contents of the flight manual and POH; environmental conditions that represent VMC; day VFR flight rules; relevant sections of the AIP.

A6 Manage abnormal situations – single-engine aeroplanes

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to accurately assess an abnormal situation, reconfigure the aeroplane, control the aeroplane and execute appropriate manoeuvres to achieve a safe outcome with no injury to personnel or damage to the aeroplane or property.

Elements and performance criteria **A6.1 – Manage engine failure – take-off (simulated)** correctly identify an engine failure after take-off; apply the highest priority to taking action to control the aeroplane; maintain control of aeroplane; perform recall actions; perform emergency actions as far as time permits; manoeuvre the aeroplane to achieve the safest possible outcome; ensure passengers adopt brace position; advise others such as ATS and other aircraft of intentions if time permits. **A6.2 – Manage engine failure in the circuit area (simulated)** correctly identify an engine failure during flight; apply the highest priority to taking action to control the aeroplane; perform recall actions; select a suitable landing area within gliding distance, on the aerodrome or elsewhere; perform emergency procedures and land the aeroplane if the engine cannot be restarted as time permits; advise ATS or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions; re-brief passengers about flight situation, brace position and harness security; land the aeroplane ensuring safest outcome if an engine restart is not achieved. **A6.3 – Perform forced landing (simulated)** after a simulated complete engine failure has occurred, without prior indications, carryout the following: identify complete power failure condition and control aeroplane; perform immediate actions; formulate and describe a recovery plan, including selecting the most suitable landing area; establish optimal gliding flight path to position the aeroplane for a landing on the selected landing area; perform emergency procedures and land the aeroplane if the engine cannot be restarted as time permits; advise ATS or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions; re-brief passengers about flight situation, brace position and harness security; land the aeroplane ensuring safest outcome if an engine restart is not achieved; after a simulated partial engine failure has occurred, without prior indications, carryout the following: identify partial power failure condition; perform recall actions; adjust flight controls to re-establish flight path that maximises performance for partial power condition and maintain a safe airspeed margin above stall speed; establish radio communications where possible; perform partial engine failure actions; formulate a plan to recover aeroplane to a safe landing area or aerodrome, taking into account that partial failure might lead to a full power failure at any time; manoeuvre the aeroplane to a selected landing area or aerodrome using the remaining power to establish an optimal aircraft position for a safe landing; advise ATS, or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions; re-brief passengers about flight situation, brace position and harness security; maintain a contingency plan for coping with a full power failure throughout the manoeuvre; when a safe landing position is established, shut down and secure engine and aeroplane. **A6.4 – Conduct precautionary search and landing (simulated condition)** assess flight circumstances and make an appropriate decision when to perform precautionary landing; configure aeroplane for conditions; perform precautionary search procedure; select landing area, carryout an inspection and assess its suitability for landing, taking into account: unobstructed approach and overshoot paths; landing area length adequate for landing; landing area surface is suitable for aeroplane type and clear of hazards; maintain orientation and visual contact with the landing area; advise ATS or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions; re-brief passengers about flight situation, brace position and harness security; land and secure aircraft and manage passengers. **A6.5 – Manage other abnormal situations (simulated)** correctly identify the situation and maintain safe control of the aeroplane at all times; manage abnormal and emergency situations in accordance with relevant emergency procedures and regulatory requirements; follow appropriate emergency procedures while maintaining control of the aeroplane; identify and conduct flight with an unreliable airspeed indication; correctly identify when an emergency evacuation of an aeroplane is required; execute a simulated emergency evacuation of an aeroplane; advise ATS or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions. **A6.6 – Recover from unusual flight attitudes** identify nose-high or nose-low unusual attitude flight condition; recover from nose-low or nose-high unusual attitudes by adjusting pitch, bank and power to resume controlled and balanced flight; apply controlled corrective action while maintaining aircraft performance within limits.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; single-engine aeroplane with piston or turbine powerplant and propeller; discontinue simulated manoeuvres that would be terminated by a forced landing when the assessor is satisfied that the landing standard would be achieved; day VFR conditions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: engine failure scenarios and procedures for partial and complete power loss; forced landing scenarios and procedures; causes leading to precautionary landings; judging descent profiles in various configurations; prioritising activities during emergencies and non-normal situations; ditching; suitable fields for forced landings and precautionary landings; considerations when practicing emergencies and non-normal operations; aircraft performance in a glide (straight and turning); hazard of sideslip at low altitude; effects of partial engine power on performance, flight profile, range and landing options; contents of the flight manual and pilot’s operating handbook; passenger control and briefing; VMC; low-flying hazards.

AME Operate multi-engine aeroplane

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to operate a multi-engine class-rated aeroplane in non-normal and emergency operations.

Elements and performance criteria **AME.1 – Operate multi-engine aeroplane** start multi-engine aeroplane; use asymmetric thrust to assist with taxi manoeuvring; check multi-engine specific systems and instrumentation. **AME.2 – Manage failures and malfunctions – general** operate and manage aircraft systems; asymmetric operations for all phases of flight are anticipated and contingencies are planned; a plan of action is self-briefed or briefed that will ensure the safest outcome in the event of asymmetric operations. **AME.3 – Manage engine failure and malfunction after take-off (simulated)** manage simulated engine failures and malfunctions effectively whilst maintaining control of the aircraft flight path within specified tolerances; configure and fly aeroplane to achieve best performance; replan flight and take action to return to land or divert to alternate. **AME.4 – Manage engine failure and malfunction en route (simulated)** maintain or regain control of the aeroplane flight path within specified tolerances; manage failed or malfunctioning engine effectively; replan flight and take action to continue or divert to alternate. **AME.5 – Perform rejected take-off – multi-engine aeroplane** abort take-off at or before decision point during the take-off where the abort procedure can be initiated and the aeroplane stopped on the remaining runway or stopway; reduce power smoothly and promptly; activate spoilers, prop fine, reverse, thrust reverse, wheel brakes and other drag and braking devices (as applicable); maintain positive control to bring the aeroplane to a safe stop; initiate and complete engine failure procedures and checklists. **AME.6 – Manage engine failure and malfunction during approach and landing (simulated)** maintain control of aeroplane flight path; nominate decision height for landing; make decision to continue or abort approach and landing in a safe and timely way; advise ATS or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions; establish the approach and landing configuration appropriate for the runway or landing area, and meteorological conditions, and adjust the power plant controls as required; maintain a stabilised approach and nominated airspeed within tolerances; achieve a smooth, positively-controlled transition from final approach to touchdown in the touchdown zone within tolerances; maintain positive directional control and cross-wind corrections during the after-landing roll maintaining the centreline within tolerances; use spoilers, prop reverse, thrust reversers, wheel brakes, and other drag or braking devices, as appropriate, in such a manner to bring the airplane to a safe stop after landing (as applicable). **AME.7 – Conduct go-around or missed approach with engine failure (simulated)** identify and confirm engine failure in a multi-engine aeroplane during a go-around or missed approach; maintain control of aeroplane; perform engine inoperative go-around safely not below the decision height.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR or IFR; class-rated multi-engine aeroplane with dual controls, electronic intercom and dual control brakes; aerodromes; appropriate surfaces; simulated emergencies; simulated hazardous weather.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: airspeed limitations, including: VNO, VA, VX and VY, VNE, VFE, VLO, VLE, VLO2 (landing gear operations down), maximum cross-wind, turbulence penetration speed and maximum load factor; emergency airspeeds, including: VMCA, VSSE, engine(s) inoperative climb, approach and final speed, emergency descent and best glide range speeds; emergency procedures for: engine failure after take-off, engine fire on the ground and airborne, engine failure in the cruise, waste gate failure (if applicable) and propeller or turbine over-speed; safety implications of asymmetric flight below VMCA; power, flight and configuration requirements that apply to VMCA; methods of regaining control of an aeroplane with a failed engine that is flying at a speed less than VMCA; conditions that would increase V1 (if stated in AFM and POH); performance the aeroplane can achieve after reaching VY or V2 during asymmetric flight; markings on the airspeed indicator that apply to failed engine operations; normal and cross-wind take-off and landing procedures: climb, cruise, descent procedures, including airspeeds, configurations, method of drift allowance, setting of flight instruments and non-normal and emergency procedures; technique and procedures used during engine failure on take-off, the appropriate reference airspeeds, and the specific pilot actions required; technique and procedure for carrying out a rejected take-off after an engine or system(s) failure or warnings, including related safety factors; technique and procedures used to conduct an asymmetric go-around or missed approach, the appropriate reference airspeeds, and the specific pilot actions required; other abnormal or emergency items as contained in the flight manual or pilot operating handbook.

TR-CR Type rating – cruise relief aeroplane

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required for the issue of a cruise-relief type rating.

Elements and performance criteria **TR-CR.1 – Conduct pre-flight inspection** complete pre-flight inspections; communicate with ground support crew; ensure all aircraft locking devices and bungs are removed; prepare and operate aircraft systems correctly. **TR-CR.2 – Extract pre-flight performance data** extract correct aircraft loading and performance data; set instrumentation and systems; obtain and interpret the take-off and departure clearance issued by ATC. **TR-CR.3 – Request ATC clearance**

Obtain, interpret and brief ATC clearance.

**TR-CR.4 – Start engines** start engine correctly; manage occurrences where specific instructions or checklist items are not published.

**TR-CR.5 – Taxi aircraft** request ATC clearances or make mandatory air traffic broadcast; push back or power back aircraft safely; maintain control of aircraft during taxi; divide attention appropriately between inside and outside the flight deck, to ensure maintenance of control while taxiing and completion of cockpit procedures and checklists; check instruments in a suitable area clear of traffic and other hazards; interpret and comply with taxiway, lighting, other aerodrome markings and marshalling instructions; adjust taxi speed to suit aircraft type, surface conditions, congestion, and maintenance of control, and avoid collision with personnel, obstacles or other aircraft; apply flying controls, power and brakes to maintain the aircraft on the taxiway centreline while compensating for wind and surface conditions.

**TR-CR.6 – Conduct pre-take-off checks** perform pre-take-off checklist and confirm all systems are within normal operating range; perform pre-take-off briefing; confirm, prior to entering runway, that aircraft is positioned on specified or appropriate taxiway; ensure final approach path is clear of conflicting traffic on specified or appropriate runway.

**TR-CR.7 – Conduct take-off** demonstrate knowledge of airspeeds, configurations, and emergency and abnormal procedures for normal and cross-wind take-offs; brief a plan of action to ensure the safest outcome in the event of abnormal operations; verify and correctly apply correction for the existing wind component to the take-off performance; ensure all pre-take-off checks required by the appropriate checklist items are completed in a timely manner; align the aircraft on the runway centreline; apply the controls correctly to maintain longitudinal alignment on the centreline of the runway, if appropriate, prior to initiating and during the take-off; adjust the power plant controls; monitor power plant controls, settings, and instruments during take-off to ensure all predetermined parameters are maintained; adjust the controls to attain the desired pitch attitude at the predetermined airspeed to attain the desired performance; perform the required pitch changes and, as appropriate, perform and verify the completion of, gear and flap retractions, power adjustments (as applicable) and other required pilot‑related activities at the required airspeed within the published tolerances; use the applicable noise abatement and wake turbulence avoidance procedures; verify the completion of the appropriate after take-off checklist items in a timely manner; manage any incident, malfunction or failure during take-off to achieve the safest possible outcome.

**TR-CR.8 – Operate aircraft in flight** operate aircraft in normal flight profiles; operate aircraft systems for normal, non-normal and emergency conditions; demonstrate the following manoeuvres: approach to stall and full stall recovery; maximum performance turning; unusual attitude and upset recovery; flight with unreliable airspeed; emergency descent.

**TR-CR.9 – Manage engine failure in flight** maintain control of aircraft flight path; correctly identify and verify malfunction; manage failure effectively.

**TR-CR.10 – Conduct a descent, arrival and landing** plan and conduct a descent, arrival and landing; obtain, interpret and brief ATC clearance for descent and arrival; manage non-normal or emergency conditions; demonstrate missed approach manoeuvre.

**TR-CR.11 – Conduct taxi to stand, park and shutdown**

Follow published procedures, taxi, park and shutdown aircraft at the designated parking bay.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day and night VMC or IMC; approved aircraft or approved flight simulation training device; simulated abnormal or emergency situations; flight crew incapacitation (multi-crew operations); simulated hazardous weather; sealed, gravel or grass surfaces.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: normal and cross-wind take-off; instrument take-off; engine failure during take-off; the procedures used during engine failure on take-off, the appropriate reference airspeeds, and the specific pilot actions required; rejected take-off; departure procedures; steep turns; approaches to stalls; engine failure; any specific flight characteristics; recovery from unusual attitudes; normal and cross-wind approaches and landings; approach and landing with a (simulated) engine failure; baulked approach and missed-landing; no flap or a non-standard flap approach and landing; critical airspeeds, V-speeds (including tyre rotation limits); how to calculate landing distance required; the normal system operating procedures of the aircraft systems; emergency procedures; how potential, kinetic and chemical energy relate to an aircraft in flight; how energy states are manipulated to generate aerodynamic forces that allow an aircraft to be manoeuvred; the unintended flight conditions of pitch, bank and airspeed that describe upset aircraft state; the physical symptoms that may or may not be evident in a stall; stall recovery technique during any nominated phase of flight applicable to the aircraft type being flown; the upset recovery techniques applicable to the aircraft type being flown at low altitude, and high altitude where the aircraft is pressurised; Structural integrity of an aeroplane is not ensured when operating at or below maximum manoeuvring speed, if multiple control inputs in one axis, or full control inputs in more than one axis, are initiated at the same time.

TR-SEA Type rating – single-engine aeroplane

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required for a person to operate a type-rated single‑engine aeroplane.

Elements and performance criteria **TR-SEA.1 – Conduct pre-flight inspection** complete pre-flight inspection correctly; communicate effectively with ground support crew; ensure all aircraft locking devices, covers and bungs are removed; prepare and operate aircraft systems. **TR-SEA.2 – Extract pre-flight performance data** extract correct aircraft loading and performance data; set instrumentation and systems; obtain and interpret the take-off and departure clearance issued by ATC. **TR-SEA.3 – Request ATC clearance**

Obtain, interpret and brief ATC clearance.

**TR-SEA.4 – Start engine** start engine; manage occurrences where specific instructions or checklist items are not published.

**TR-SEA.5 – Taxi aircraft** request ATC clearances or make mandatory air traffic broadcast appropriate to the local airspace and aerodrome; maintain control of aircraft during taxi; divide attention appropriately between inside and outside the flight deck, to ensure aircraft control is maintained while taxiing and complete cockpit procedures and checklists; check instruments in a suitable area clear of traffic and other hazards; interpret and comply with taxiway, lighting, other aerodrome markings and marshalling instructions; adjust taxi speed to suit aircraft type, surface conditions, congestion, and maintenance of control; and avoid collision with personnel, obstacles or other aircraft; apply flying controls, power and brakes to maintain the aircraft on the taxiway centreline while compensating for wind and surface conditions.

**TR-SEA.6 – Conduct pre-take-off checks** perform pre-take-off checklist and confirm all systems are within normal operating range; perform pre-take-off briefing effectively; confirm prior to entering runway, that aircraft is positioned on specified or appropriate taxiway; ensure final approach path is clear of conflicting traffic on specified or appropriate runway.

**TR-SEA.7 – Conduct take-off** apply correct airspeeds, configurations, and emergency and abnormal procedures for normal and cross-wind take‑offs; conduct a briefing covering the plan of action that will ensure the safest outcome in the event of abnormal operations; verify and correctly apply correction for the existing wind component to the take-off performance; perform and ensure all pre-take-off checks required by the appropriate checklist items are completed in a timely manner; align the aircraft on the runway centreline; apply the controls correctly to maintain longitudinal alignment on the centreline of the runway, if appropriate, prior to initiating and during the take-off; adjust the powerplant controls correctly; monitor powerplant controls, settings, and instruments during take-off to ensure all predetermined parameters are maintained; adjust the controls to attain the desired pitch attitude to attain the desired performance; perform the required pitch changes and, as appropriate, perform and verify the completion of, gear and flap retractions, power adjustments (as applicable) and other required pilot‑related activities at the required airspeed within the published tolerances; use the applicable noise abatement and wake turbulence avoidance procedures, as applicable; verify the completion of the appropriate after take-off checklist items in a timely manner.

**TR-SEA.8 – Incident, malfunction or failure during take-off**

Appropriately manage incident, malfunction or failure during take-off.

**TR-SEA.9 – Operate aircraft in flight** operate aircraft in normal flight profiles; operate aircraft systems for normal, non-normal and emergency conditions; identify aeroplane upset conditions and take appropriate action to return aeroplane to normal flight; demonstrate approach to the stall and stall recovery as follows: recognises approaching stall symptoms; reduce AOA at the stall; prevents yaw with rudder; apply recommended power; when the wings are unstalled, level them using balanced aileron control; recover height loss; demonstrate maximum performance turning under the following conditions: maximum rate; minimum radius; demonstrate flight with unreliable airspeed; demonstrate ability to recover from unusual attitude and upset situations; demonstrate an emergency descent.

**TR-SEA.10 – Manage partial and complete engine failure situations in flight** maintain control of aircraft; correctly identify and verify failure; manage failure to achieve safest possible outcome; perform forced landing; perform precautionary landing (simulated).

**TR-SEA.11 – Conduct engine relight and restart in flight**

Maintain control while performing relight and restart.

**TR-SEA.12 – Conduct a descent, arrival and landing** plan and conduct a descent, arrival and landing; obtain, interpret and brief ATC clearance for descent and arrival; manage non-normal or emergency conditions; demonstrate missed approach manoeuvre.

**TR-SEA.13 – Conduct taxi to stand, park and shutdown** taxi, park and shut down aircraft at the designated parking bay as cleared; secure aircraft.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day and night VMC or IMC; upset conditions include the following: pitch attitude more than 25° nose up; pitch attitude more than 10° nose down; bank angle more than 45°; flying at airspeeds inappropriate to the conditions; aircraft of the type to which the rating applies; approved flight simulator.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: normal and cross-wind take-off; instrument take-off (IFR pilots only); engine failure during take-off; rejected take-off; departure procedures; steep turns; approaches to stalls; engine failure; any specific flight characteristics (e.g. Dutch roll); recovery from unusual attitudes; normal and cross-wind approaches and landings; approach and landing with a (simulated) engine failure – multi-engine aeroplane; baulked approach and missed landing; no flap and non-standard flap approach and landing: factors that affect an aircraft when full or partial flaps, leading edge flaps, and any other similar devices become inoperative, including aircraft handling; extract critical airspeeds, V-speeds (including tyre rotation limits); calculate landing distance required; normal systems operating procedures; emergency procedures; how potential and kinetic energy relate to an aircraft in flight; how energy states are manipulated to generate aerodynamic forces that allow an aircraft to be manoeuvred; the unintended flight conditions of pitch, bank and airspeed that describe upset aircraft state; the physical symptoms that may or may not be evident in a stall; stall recovery technique during any nominated phase of flight applicable to the aircraft type being flown; upset recovery techniques applicable to the aircraft type being flown at low altitude, and high altitude where the aircraft is pressurised; Structural integrity of an aeroplane is not ensured when operating at or below maximum manoeuvring speed, if multiple control inputs in one axis, or full control inputs in more than one axis, are initiated at the same time.

FR-SEAC SINGLE-ENGINE AEROPLANE CLASS RATING FLIGHT REVIEW

Unit description

This unit describes the standards required for a single-engine aeroplane class rating flight review.

Elements and performance criteria **FR-SEAC.1 – Conduct flight** start and taxi aircraft ready for take-off; perform a normal take-off simulating minimum take-off distance available; perform departure from circuit area; perform general handling manoeuvres, including the following: initiate stall and recover where initial symptoms of a stall become evident; perform a full stall and recovery; perform steep level and descending turns through at least 360°; conduct low flying at 500 ft AGL and perform a reversal turn; perform circuit rejoin and at least 1 full circuit pattern; perform a missed approach; perform a flapless approach and landing; perform cross-wind take-off and landing if conditions permit; perform a normal landing simulating minimum landing distance available. **FR-SEAC.2 – Manage aircraft systems** ensure sufficient fuel is loaded and fuel consumption is monitored and managed throughout the flight; manage the aircraft fuel system; manage all other aircraft systems. **FR-SEAC.3 – Navigation (optional)** plan flight of at least 3 legs and submit flight plan in accordance with AIP; conduct a departure; navigate en route using visual and instrument navigation systems; perform diversion procedure; conduct arrival. **FR-SEAC.4 – Airspace** comply with airspace procedures and requirements; operate aircraft radio and conform to standard radio procedures. **FR-SEAC.5 – Instrument flying** perform basic flight manoeuvres using full instrument panel; recover from upset situations and unusual aircraft attitudes to straight and level flight; perform checks and monitor system for serviceability. **FR-SEAC.6 – Manage non-normal and emergency conditions** manage a simulated engine failure in the take-off segment (optional); manage a simulated partial engine failure (optional); manage a simulated complete engine failure and execute a forced landing; manage aircraft system malfunctions other than engine failure. **FR-SEAC.7 – Non-technical skills** recognise and manage threats and errors during pre-flight planning and in-flight; maintain effective lookout and situational awareness; assess situations and make appropriate decisions; set priorities and manage tasks; maintain effective communication with stakeholders; communicate effectively using aeronautical radio. **FR-SEAC.8 – Manage passengers and cargo** conduct pre-flight and in-flight safety briefings to ensure passengers are familiar with safety procedures, emergency equipment, exits and operational requirements; manage cargo.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; simulated conditions can be used; for FR-SEAC.5 – instrument flying, simulated or actual instrument conditions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: privileges, limitations and responsibilities of the licences, ratings and endorsements the applicant holds; flight review requirements; obtaining, interpreting and applying meteorological and aeronautical information; navigation and flight planning for day VFR operations; weight and balance and aircraft performance; operation of systems fitted to the aircraft that is used in the flight review; extracting and applying aircraft performance data, including take-off and landing performance data for the aircraft that is used in the flight review; airspace requirements and procedures; manage cargo and passengers; hazard identification and risk management; non-normal and emergency procedures, including full and partial failures; local operating procedures; hazardous weather; airworthiness requirements; reporting requirements; ERSA normal and emergency procedures; current and recently changed legislation and procedures that are relevant to the applicant’s licences, ratings and endorsements.

FR-MEAC Multi-engine aeroplane class rating flight review

Unit description

This unit describes the standards required for a multi-engine aeroplane class rating flight review.

Elements and performance criteria **FR-MEAC.1 – Conduct flight** start and taxi aircraft ready for take-off; perform a normal take-off simulating minimal take-off distance available; perform departure from circuit area; perform general handling manoeuvres, including the following: initiate stall and recover where initial symptoms of a stall become evident; perform a full stall and recovery; perform steep level and descending turns through at least 360°; conduct low flying at 500 ft AGL and perform a reversal turn; perform circuit rejoin and at least 1 full circuit pattern; perform a missed approach; perform a normal landing simulating minimum landing distance available. **FR-MEAC.2 – Manage aircraft systems** ensure sufficient fuel is loaded and fuel consumption is monitored and managed throughout the flight; manage the aircraft fuel system; manage all other aircraft systems. **FR-MEAC.3 – Navigation (optional)** plan flight of at least 3 legs and submit flight plan in accordance with AIP; conduct a departure; navigate en route using visual and instrument navigation systems; perform diversion procedure; conduct arrival. **FR-MEAC.4 – Airspace** comply with airspace procedures and requirements; operate aircraft radio and conform to standard radio procedures. **FR-MEAC.5 – Instrument flying** perform basic flight manoeuvres using full instrument panel; recover from upset situations and unusual aircraft attitudes to straight and level flight; perform checks and monitor system for serviceability. **FR-MEAC.6 – Manage non-normal and emergency conditions** manage a simulated engine failure in the take-off segment; manage a simulated partial engine failure; manage a simulated complete engine failure and execute a simulated asymmetric approach and landing; manage aircraft system malfunctions. **FR-MEAC.7 – Non-technical skills** recognise and manage threats and errors during pre-flight planning and in-flight; maintain effective lookout and situational awareness; assess situations and make appropriate decisions; set priorities and manage tasks; maintain effective communication with stakeholders; communicate effectively using aeronautical radio. **FR-MEAC.8 – Manage passengers and cargo.** conduct pre-flight and in-flight safety briefings to ensure passengers are familiar with safety procedures, emergency equipment, exits and operational requirements; manage cargo.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; simulated conditions can be used; for FR-MEAC.5 – instrument flying, simulated or actual instrument conditions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: privileges, limitations and responsibilities of the licences, ratings and endorsements the applicant holds; flight review requirements; obtaining, interpreting and applying meteorological and aeronautical information; navigation and flight planning for day VFR operations; weight and balance and aircraft performance; operation of systems fitted to the aircraft that is used in the flight review; extracting and applying aircraft performance data, including take-off and landing performance date for the aircraft that is used in the flight review; airspace requirements and procedures; manage cargo and passengers; hazard identification and risk management; non-normal and emergency procedures, including full and partial failures; local operating procedures; hazardous weather; airworthiness requirements; reporting requirements; ERSA normal and emergency procedures; current and recently changed legislation and procedures that are relevant to the applicant’s licences, ratings and endorsements.

FR-MEAT Multi-engine aeroplane type rating flight review

recover from upset situations and unusual aircraft attitudes to straight and level flight; perform checks and monitor system for serviceability. **FR- MEAT.6 – Manage non-normal and emergency conditions** manage a simulated engine failure in the take-off segment;
