Underpinning knowledge of the following: privileges, limitations and responsibilities of the licences, ratings and endorsements the applicant holds; flight review requirements; obtaining, interpreting and applying meteorological and aeronautical information; navigation and flight planning for day VFR operations; weight and balance and aircraft performance; operation of systems fitted to the aircraft that is used in the flight review; extracting and applying aircraft performance data, including take-off and landing performance date for the aircraft that is used in the flight review; airspace requirements and procedures; manage cargo and passengers; hazard identification and risk management; non-normal and emergency procedures, including full and partial failures; local operating procedures; hazardous weather; airworthiness requirements; reporting requirements; ERSA normal and emergency procedures; current and recently changed legislation and procedures that are relevant to the applicant’s licences, ratings and endorsements.

TR-FE Type rating – flight engineer

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required by a flight engineer to operate a type-rated aircraft.

Elements and performance criteria **FTM.1 – Conduct pre-flight inspection** complete pre-flight inspection correctly; communicate effectively with ground support crew; ensure removal of appropriate aircraft engine protective devices; prepare and operate aircraft systems. **FTM.2 – Manage engines** manage engine systems correctly; manage and monitor aircraft systems as appropriate; manage occurrences where specific instructions or checklist items are not published. **FTM.3 – Conduct pre-take-off checks** complete the pre-take-off checklist and confirm all applicable systems are within normal operating range. **FTM.4 – Conduct take-off** operate flight engineer controls correctly; adjust the power plant controls correctly; monitor power plant controls, settings, and instruments during take-off to ensure all predetermined parameters are maintained; inform the pilot in command of abnormal or emergency situations in a timely manner. **FTM.5 – Operate aircraft in flight** operate flight engineer systems for normal, non-normal and emergency conditions; identify an aeroplane upset condition and immediately informs the pilot in command. **FTM.6 – Manage engine failure in flight** inform pilot in command; correctly identify and verify failed engine; manage failure appropriately. **FTM.7 – Conducts engine relight and restart in flight FTM.8 – Conducts shutdown** The person must be able to demonstrate her or his ability to correctly shutdown the aircraft.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day and night VMC or IMC; upset conditions include the following: pitch attitude more than 25° nose up; pitch attitude more than 10° nose down; bank angle more than 45°; flying at airspeeds inappropriate to the conditions. approved multi-engine multi-crew aircraft; approved flight simulator; simulated abnormal or emergency situations; flight crew incapacitation (multi-crew operations); simulated hazardous weather.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: engine failure during take-off; rejected take-off; departure procedures; aircraft systems failures; any specific flight characteristics (e.g. Dutch roll); recognition of unusual attitudes; recognition of aeroplane upset conditions (aeroplane only); normal systems operating procedures; emergency procedures; approach and landing with a (simulated) engine failure – multi-engine aircraft.

HELICOPTER CATEGORY

H1 Control helicopter on the ground – stationary

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to operate a stationary helicopter on the ground.

Elements and performance criteria **H1.1 – Start and stop engine** ensure the helicopter is in a suitable location for starting the engine and rotors; perform pre-start and start actions; perform shutdown and after-shutdown actions; control blade sailing during start and shut down by appropriate positioning of helicopter and use of cyclic pitch; comply with manufacturer’s limitations and report deviations when appropriate; manage emergencies appropriately (simulated). **H1.2 – Engage rotor** set engine RPM within limits before rotor engagement (if applicable – this is only relevant to the few rotorcraft, including the R22 and R44 which are the most common basic trainers); engage rotor correctly (if applicable); maintain engine RPM within limits during rotor engagement; maintain disc position within operating limits as Rotor RPM (RRPM) increases; operate rotor brake correctly (if applicable – this is only relevant to the very few rotocraft that can run 1 engine at idle before rotor engagement); monitor and react appropriately to transmission, hydraulic system and engine indications (if applicable). **H1.3 – Control main rotor disc and anti-torque system** maintain the correct main rotor disc attitude during all RRPM operations; set correct engine idle RPM; set correct anti-torque pedal position to compensate for main rotor torque; maintain correct rotor disc attitude and RRPM while performing other tasks or actions.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; helicopter with dual controls and electronic intercom, if fitted; engine start and shutdown emergencies covered by the aircraft flight manual; malfunctions and emergency procedures described in the flight manual; day VFR; aerodromes and helicopter landing sites; obstructions and personnel (simulated); various wind conditions (may be simulated).

Underpinning knowledge of the following: regulations and procedures relating to the ground operation of rotorcraft; operational and start limitations of typical helicopters; applicable helicopter systems; operating on different surfaces, including sealed and unsealed surfaces; effect of wind on rotor blade control (blade sailing); use of the fire extinguisher system fitted to the helicopter; ground resonance; dynamic rollover; local noise abatement procedures and curfews.

H2 Control helicopter in lift-off, hover and landing

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to complete pre-take-off checks, lift-off helicopter to the hover, complete hover checks, perform hover, perform aborted lift-off, perform hovering turns and land from the hover.

Elements and performance criteria **H2.1 – Lift-off and hover helicopter, perform hover checks and abort take-off** calculate aircraft performance for the flight; complete pre-take-off checks; lift-off helicopter: set flight controls correctly to prepare for lift-off to the hover at the location; use correct flight and power controls to lift helicopter off the surface to a stable hover at the appropriate hover height for the helicopter while controlling heading; anticipate and take account of wind effect with appropriate control inputs to maintain position over hover point; demonstrate awareness of rotor downwash on surrounding aircraft, people, objects and environment; confirm the proper functioning of the flight controls and the centre of gravity and power required to hover are within limits; at a constant and safe hover height, commence, maintain and stop a hover taxi manoeuvre while maintaining power and RRPM within the limits; remain clear of the manufacturer’s ‘height-velocity diagram avoid area’ when applicable; perform aborted take-off from the hover. **H2.2 – Hover helicopter in cross-wind and tailwind** maintain helicopter in flight over a nominated hover point at a nominated height and heading in cross-wind and tailwind; apply controlled corrective action to maintain a constant rate of turn and counter the effects of wind. **H2.3 – Perform turn around a mast** turn helicopter around a mast while maintaining a constant height at a constant rate of turn using anti-torque pedals; stop the turn on a nominated heading; maintain RPM within limits during the turn. **H2.4 – Perform turns around nose and tail** turn helicopter around a nominated point on or forward of the nose while maintaining a constant height and specified rate of movement around the point; turn helicopter around a nominated point on or aft of the tail while maintaining a constant height and specified rate of movement around the point; commence turns in a specified direction and stop them at a specified heading; maintain RPM within limits during the turn; maintain ground track at a constant distance from the nominated point; use the anti-torque pedals to ensure helicopter is pointed at the nominated turning point. **H2.5 – Perform sideways and backwards flight** transition from static hover to forward, sideways and backwards flight and terminate this movement over a nominated hover point at a nominated height; ensure direction of travel is clear of obstructions; conduct backward movement only after visually checking behind helicopter and adjusting height as required; maintain sideways and backwards directional control; maintain RPM within limits during the turn; maintain rate of movement of helicopter at a safe speed; maintain lookout in direction of travel; terminate sideways or backwards movement at desired hover point. **H2.6 – Land from the hover** complete pre-landing checks (if applicable); nominate touchdown point; from a stable hover, establish a controlled rate of descent, maintain heading and remain over the nominated hover point; land helicopter at a suitable rate and maintain a constant heading without lateral or longitudinal drift while maintaining the requisite RRPM during the landing sequence; ensure helicopter is stable on its undercarriage prior to fully lowering collective; perform after-landing checks; for mishandled landing: recognise when a safe landing cannot be achieved; discontinue the landing and return to the hover safely; re-establish a stabilised hover; land from the stabilised hover.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; helicopter with dual controls and electronic intercom day VFR; aerodromes and helicopter landing sites; obstructions and personnel (simulated); various wind conditions (may be simulated).

Underpinning knowledge of the following: calculates aircraft performance for the flight; operational and start limitations of typical helicopters; operating on different surfaces, including sealed and unsealed surfaces; effect of wind on rotor blade control (blade sailing); use of the fire extinguisher system fitted to the helicopter being used; ground resonance; recirculation; dynamic rollover; local noise abatement procedures and curfews.

H3 Taxi helicopter

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to taxi a helicopter.

Elements and performance criteria **H.3.1 – Ground taxi helicopter** use correct flight and power control techniques to initiate forward movement of the helicopter on the surface; check and confirm the proper functioning of the wheel brake system; use correct flight and power control techniques to ground taxi and manoeuvre the helicopter on appropriate surfaces (wet and dry) at a safe speed in headwind, cross-wind and tailwind conditions; perform flight instrument checks while taxiing (if applicable); avoids adverse effects of rotor wash on personnel, aircraft, structures and loose objects; apply smooth control while ground taxiing and manoeuvring the helicopter with turns at a constant and safe rate of turn while maintaining power and RRPM within the limits; adjusts taxi speed to suit helicopter type, surface conditions, congestion while maintaining control and desired track and avoiding collision with obstacles and other aircraft; maintain landing gear in contact with the ground; apply smooth and controlled actions to terminate at a nominated holding or parking point under different wind and surface conditions; maintain RRPM within normal operating limits; observe mast operating limits, if applicable; ensure final approach path is clear of conflicting traffic. **H3.2 – Air taxi helicopter** manoeuvre the helicopter while allowing for prevailing conditions, over a prescribed track at a constant height; maintain alignment of the landing gear with the direction of travel; remain clear of manufacturer’s ‘height-velocity diagram avoid area’; maintain RPM within operating limits; adjust air taxi speed to suit helicopter type, traffic conditions, congestion, and maintenance of control and to avoid collision with obstacles or other aircraft; ensure final approach path is clear of conflicting traffic. **H3.3 – Air transit helicopter** obtain transit clearance and complies with ATC instructions (if applicable); manoeuvre the helicopter, while allowing for prevailing conditions, over a prescribed track at a height not above 100 ft AGL at airspeeds greater than speeds used for air taxiing; limits movement within the aerodrome boundaries, without incident; remain clear of manufacturer’s ‘height-velocity diagram avoid area’; maintain height; manipulate instruments, switches or devices, when safe to do so, including when the release of the collective pitch level is required, while maintaining height, heading, speed, and attitude and not exceeding RPM or power limits; avoid conditions that could lead to loss of tail rotor or anti-torque effectiveness; aligns helicopter with track, or balances, as applicable; adjust air transit ground speed to suit helicopter type, traffic conditions, congestion, and maintenance of control and to avoid collision with obstacles or other aircraft; maintain RRPM within normal operating limits; avoid adverse effect of rotor wash on other aircraft, facilities, loose objects and personnel; ensure final approach path is clear of conflicting traffic.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; helicopter with dual controls and electronic intercom; day VFR; aerodromes and helicopter landing sites; obstructions and personnel (simulated); various wind conditions (may be simulated).

Underpinning knowledge of the following: height-velocity diagram; adverse effects of rotor wash; ground resonance and action to be taken when it occurs; taxiway and runway markings; loss of tail rotor effectiveness and action to be taken when it occurs; hazards and risks associated with conducting air taxi and air transit manoeuvres.

H4 Take-off helicopter and approach to hover

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to prepare a helicopter for take-off, perform take-off and perform an approach to termination at hover.

Elements and performance criteria **H4.1 – Carryout pre-take-off checks** complete pre-take-off checks correctly and clearing turn (if applicable); assess situation and select safe take-off path; conduct a take-off safety briefing (this may be carried out prior to take off lift-off to the hover if necessitated by location); clear the area, taxi into the take-off position, perform line-up checks. **H4.2 – Take-off helicopter** transition to forward flight and maintain take-off path; recognise and control translational lift effect; accelerate to and maintain the recommended or nominated climb speed; control the helicopter to remain outside of the Height-Velocity (H-V) avoid curve, balanced and trimmed (if applicable); ensure obstacle clearance; correct power and attitude are maintained for the profile and IAS to be flown; landing gear is retracted after a positive rate of climb is established (if applicable); comply with noise abatement procedures, where applicable; complete after take-off checks. **H4.3 – Approach to hover** select a suitable termination point; complete checklists as applicable for manoeuvre; intercept and maintain appropriate approach angle and track; adjust power and attitude to achieve a controlled decreasing closure rate to the termination point; align the landing gear to the planned approach direction; recognise and control loss of translational lift; controls RPM within limits; terminates approach to the hover over the termination point. **H4.4 – Perform go-round procedure** recognise adverse conditions that require the execution of a go-round; initiate go-round safely in the time available; set power and attitude to achieve safe climb at appropriate IAS; maintain control throughout go-round procedure; align landing gear with the planned take-off direction until the point at which balanced flight is required; perform after-take-off checks.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; helicopter with dual controls and electronic intercom; day VFR; aerodromes and helicopter landing sites; obstructions and personnel (simulated); various wind conditions (may be simulated).

Underpinning knowledge of the following: vortex ring state; loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE); low ‘g’ and mast bumping; overpitching or low RRPM – rotor stall; recirculation; contributing operational situations and environmental conditions; avoidance and recognition of and recovery techniques appropriate to helicopter type; aircraft systems; aircraft performance; aircraft weight and balance; AFM and POH; day VFR flight rules.

H5 Control helicopter in normal flight

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to control a helicopter in normal flight, whilst flying straight and level, climbing, descending and turning.

Elements and performance criteria **H5.1 – Climb helicopter** set and maintain power and attitude to establish and maintain climb flight on a constant heading for the following profiles: maintain IAS for cruise climb; maintain IAS for best angle of climb (VX); maintain IAS for best rate of climb (VY); set appropriate altimeter settings; ensure helicopter is balanced and trimmed (if applicable); maintain power as altitude increases. **H5.2 – Maintain straight and level flight** set and maintain power and attitude to achieve straight and level flight at nominated airspeeds, altitudes and headings; ensure helicopter is balanced and trimmed (if applicable). **H5.3 – Descend helicopter** set and maintain power and attitude to achieve cruise descending flight on a constant heading at a nominated rate of descent; set appropriate altimeter settings; identify and avoid terrain and aircraft traffic; ensure helicopter is balanced and trimmed (if applicable). **H5.4 – Turn helicopter** perform airspace cleared procedure; set and maintain power, attitude and bank to achieve specified turn performance to the left and to the right, onto specific headings or geographical features for the following: level turns; climbing turn, rate 1 or with 20° bank angle; powered descending turn with 30° bank angle; turn helicopter onto specified headings using the magnetic compass; manoeuvre the helicopter over specified ground tracks; ensure helicopter is balanced and trimmed (if applicable). **H5.5 – Perform circuits and approaches** plan and conduct descent; join traffic pattern; maintain a safe separation from other traffic joining, departing or in the traffic pattern; track upwind on extended centreline to 500 ft; adjust circuit to ensure spacing with preceding traffic; establish the helicopter on cross-wind tracking 90° to the runway; establish the helicopter on downwind at circuit height tracking parallel to the runway at a specified distance from the runway; perform pre-landing checks; establish aircraft on base leg a specified distance from helicopter landing site; commence and control rate of descent to maintain approach path; ensure helicopter is aligned with specified or appropriate runway when applicable; establish helicopter on final approach in approach configuration not below 500 ft AGL; select termination point; maintain closure rate to the termination point; maintain helicopter on extended centreline, approach slope and approach speed; adjust speed to compensate for wind gusts; complete final approach checks; ensure helicopter is balanced and trimmed (as applicable); complete approach at the termination point. **H5.6 – Comply with airspace requirements** use a chart and identify the geographical limits of the designated area; with reference to a suitable chart, identify prominent geographical features; describe the position of controlled airspace using a suitable chart and geographical features; identify and avoid restricted areas and controlled airspace using a chart and geographical features when applicable; complete departure from the circuit area and transits to the designated area without incident; complete departure from the designated area and transits to the circuit area without incident; maintain orientation by geographical features with the aid of a suitable map.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; helicopter with dual controls and electronic intercom; day VFR; aerodromes and helicopter landing sites; obstructions and personnel (simulated); various wind conditions (may be simulated).

Underpinning knowledge of the following: primary and secondary effects of helicopter controls; vortex ring state; circuit operations; managing non-normal and emergencies in the circuit area; wind shear, turbulence and wake turbulence; helicopter instruments and monitoring helicopter performance.

H6 Control helicopter during advanced manoeuvres

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to control a helicopter during advanced manoeuvres and procedures.

Elements and performance criteria **H6.1 – Turn helicopter steeply** complete airspace cleared procedure; perform steep turns (45º) onto a nominated heading or geographical feature as follows: maintaining altitude; descending through a minimum descent of 500 ft; in balance. **H6.2 – Perform autorotative flight** enter and maintain autorotative flight at a nominated speed in balanced flight for the following profiles: straight descent at nominated heading and manufacturer’s recommended speed; turning descent through 180˚ and 360˚ using up to 45˚ angle of bank; best range speed and minimum descent rate speed; maintain RRPM within limitations during autorotative flight; perform power recovery as follows: anticipate and comply with nominated minimum descent altitude; ensure engine RPM and RRPM ‘needles’ are rejoined prior to the setting of climb power; set climb power; control yaw; set climb speed; perform power termination as follows: maintain RRPM within limitations; ensure throttle(s) is at 100% (or the equivalent terminology) prior to the commencement of the flare; commence flare at appropriate height for the prevailing conditions and reduce ground speed and rate of descent; controls attitude to achieve a decreasing closure rate and reducing rate of descent; control yaw, engine and RRPM; terminate the helicopter to a hover or hover taxi within tolerances of termination point without lateral or rearward movement; perform autorotative landing as follows: commence flare at appropriate height for the prevailing conditions and reduce ground speed and rate of descent; control RRPM; select and maintain helicopter at the hover attitude without lateral or rearward movement; control touchdown rate; control yaw; land helicopter with zero or minimum run-on speed within tolerances of nominated touchdown point without lateral or rearward movement. **H6.3 – Land on, and lift off from, sloping ground** Land on sloping ground: plan and conduct a slope landing in accordance with the wind and slope limits specified for the helicopter (if stated); use the appropriate slope landing technique relevant to the helicopter as follows: make adjustments using the controls in response to wind, surface and applicable limitations; maintain RRPM within limits; apply an appropriate rate of descent whilst maintaining a constant heading and preventing all drift during all the phases of land on; control the roll rate of the helicopter following first contact; maintain the helicopter’s position on the slope while lowering collective and centralising the cyclic; ensure security of the helicopter on the sloping surface prior to reducing rotor RPM. Lift off from sloping ground: plan and conduct a lift-off from sloping ground in accordance with the wind and slope limits of the helicopter; use the appropriate slope lift-off technique for the helicopter as follows: make adjustments using the controls in response to wind, surface and applicable limitations; maintain RRPM within limits; apply an appropriate rate of climb while maintaining a constant heading and preventing all drift during all the phases of lift-off; control the roll rate of the rotorcraft during lift-off; establish a stable hover above the lift off position clear of all obstacles. **H6.4 – Land, take off and manoeuvre in a confined area** Land in confined area: plan and conduct a confined area landing in accordance with the limitations for the helicopter; confirm helicopter performance, which includes power checks as applicable; inspect confined area and determine a plan, including an appropriate approach and departure path; intercept and maintain approach path to the termination point; operate the helicopter within its limitations; land at a suitable landing and lift-off area. Take off from confined area: plan a take-off from a confined area in accordance with the limitations for the helicopter; calculate and confirm the helicopter’s take-off performance is adequate for the confined area; determine an appropriate abort point; identify all obstacles on the departure patch and a possible abort path in the confined area; conduct take-off and departure from the confined area and remain clear of obstacles with a margin that is applicable to the operation; operate the helicopter within its limitations. Manoeuvre in a confined area: plan for manoeuvring in a confined area in accordance with the limitations for the helicopter; confirm the helicopter’s performance, which includes power checks as applicable; identify all obstacles in the confined area; manoeuvre the helicopter in the confined area while remaining clear of obstacles; operate the helicopter within its limitations. **H6.5 – Execute limited power take-off, approach and landing** Limited power take-off: confirm the helicopter’s performance using its performance charts; apply maximum, or nominated, power, while maintaining optimum RRPM; accelerate helicopter at an appropriate rate; recognise and control translational lift effect; maintain direction of departure path then balance when appropriate; establish and maintain climb; identify and avoid obstacles. Limited power approach and landing: confirm the helicopter’s performance using its performance charts; confirm the landing area available is sufficient for a safe limited power approach and landing; determine an appropriate plan for approach, which includes the nomination of a suitable touchdown point; intercept the planned approach path appropriate for the performance of the helicopter in the prevailing conditions; manage the helicopter’s airspeed with the optimum RRPM appropriate to the power available and landing environment; identify and avoid obstacles; maintain effective translational lift until touchdown is assured; maintain balance and direction of approach path; touchdown on the nominated touchdown point; control the helicopter on the ground. **H6.6 – Land on, and take-off, from a pinnacle or ridgeline (CPL only)** Land on pinnacle or ridgeline: plan a pinnacle or ridgeline landing in accordance with the limitations of the helicopter; confirm the helicopter’s performance, which includes power checks as applicable; inspect the ridgeline or pinnacle as applicable, and determine a plan including an appropriate approach and departure path; assess the local environment conditions for effects of the terrain on wind and turbulence; intercept and maintain the approach path to the termination point; operate the helicopter within its limitations and set optimum RPM; maintain effective translational lift until touchdown is assured; terminate to a hover over the selected landing and lift-off area; touchdown on nominated touchdown point; control the helicopter on the ground. Take off from pinnacle or ridgeline: plan a take-off from in a pinnacle or ridgeline in accordance with the limitations of the helicopter; calculate and confirm the helicopter’s take-off performance is adequate for the departure; determine an appropriate abort point (if applicable); identify all obstacles on the departure patch and proposed abort path for the pinnacle or ridgeline (if applicable); conduct take-off and departure from the pinnacle or ridgeline remaining clear of obstacles with a margin that is applicable to the operation; operate the helicopter within its limitations.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR; where applicable: confined helicopter landing site; terrain with sloping ground; terrain with a pinnacle or ridgeline; simulated abnormal and emergency situations; simulated hazardous or marginal weather; for PPL, autorotative landings may be replaced by a power termination.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: cross-wind and rotor control limits for the helicopter; helicopter performance limitations; local weather conditions; typical hazards and risks associated with conducting advanced manoeuvres and identify precautions and procedures to control the risks; instructions, procedures and information that is relevant to executing advanced manoeuvres and procedures.

H7 Manage abnormal situations and emergencies – helicopter

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to manage abnormal and emergency situations in helicopters.

Elements and performance criteria **H7.1 – Manage forced landing from level flight** identify engine failure correctly and maintain control of helicopter; establish and maintain helicopter in autorotative flight; maintain balance; control RRPM within limitations; select suitable landing area; position helicopter to land in selected area; make appropriate radio transmissions (if time permits); perform emergency checks; brief passengers as appropriate; perform autorotative landing and secure helicopter. **H7.2 – Manage engine failure during take-off and on final approach** identify engine failure correctly and maintain control of helicopter; establish and maintain helicopter in autorotative flight; maintain skids parallel to direction of travel; perform autorotative landing or power termination and secure helicopter. **H7.3 – Manage engine failure during hover or hover taxi** During hover: correctly identify engine failure; control yaw and drift; perform controlled touchdown. During hover taxi: correctly identify engine failure; control yaw and drift; maintain skids parallel to direction of travel; perform controlled touchdown; control ground-slide. **H7.4 – Manage tail rotor malfunctions** During flight: correctly identify tail rotor malfunction; maintain control of the helicopter; select a suitable landing area; manoeuvre helicopter to a position where the safest landing is assured; land the helicopter. During hover: correctly identify tail rotor malfunction; maintain control of the helicopter; select a suitable landing area; land the helicopter. **H7.5 – Manage jammed flight control systems** correctly identify when controls are jammed; locate and remove any objects that are causing the jam; maintain control of the helicopter and rectify the malfunction, if appropriate; manoeuvre the helicopter to the safest landing area available. **H7.6 – Manage helicopter systems malfunctions** maintain control of the helicopter; identify and confirm the system malfunction; manage the malfunction appropriately; where appropriate, isolate the system; perform emergency procedures.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; helicopter with dual controls and electronic intercom; day VFR; aerodromes and helicopter landing sites; obstructions and personnel (simulated); various wind conditions (can be simulated).

Underpinning knowledge of the following: emergency procedures; applicable system malfunctions; managing system malfunctions; prioritising tasks when managing malfunctions; the following key hazards including, for each, the typical causal factors and contributing operational situations, avoidance and recognition of symptoms and recovery techniques: vortex ring state; ground resonance; loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE); low ‘g’ and mast bumping; overpitching or low RRPM – rotor stall; retreating blade stall; recirculation; dynamic rollover; the impact of high gross weight and high density altitude on key hazards; threat and error management as follows: flight planning to avoid hazardous flight regimes; techniques for how to avoid a potentially hazardous situation developing whilst in flight.

TR-SEH Type rating – single-engine helicopter

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to operate a type-rated single-engine helicopter.

Elements and performance criteria **TR-SEH.1 – Control helicopter on the ground** For all helicopters: prepare for start as follows: using an orderly procedure with checklists, inspect and prepare the helicopter, including those items recommended by the manufacturer, for a flight; identify and verify switches, circuit breakers, fuses, and spare fuses pertinent to day and night operations; confirm that there is sufficient fuel and oil for the intended flight; identify and verify the required equipment for the flight is on-board and serviceable; ensure security of baggage and required equipment; organise and arrange documents and equipment that will need to be accessed in flight in a manner that makes the items readily available; perform an effective passenger safety briefing (if type capable of carrying passengers); conduct engine start and rotor engagement as follows: ensure helicopter is located in a suitable location for starting engine and rotors; use the appropriate checklist provided by the helicopter manufacturer or owner or operator; calculate and confirm sufficient power margin available for the proposed flight; demonstrate knowledge of recommended starting procedures; take appropriate action with respect to unsatisfactory start conditions; complete the appropriate engine and helicopter systems checks; taxiing and hover manoeuvring as follows: carry out pre-take-off checks; set flight controls correctly to prepare for the lift-off transition to the hover at the location; use correct flight and power control techniques to lift helicopter off the surface to a stable hover at the appropriate hover height for the helicopter; confirm the proper functioning of the flight controls and confirm centre of gravity and power required to hover are within limits; trim helicopter where applicable; demonstrate smooth control at a constant safe hover height while hover manoeuvring and maintaining power and RRPM within the limits; maintain helicopter in flight over a nominated hover point at a nominated height and heading in cross-wind and tailwind; transition from static hover to forward, sideways and backwards flight and terminate this movement over a nominated hover point; turn helicopter around a the mast while maintaining a constant height at a constant rate of turn using anti-torque pedals; turn helicopter around a nominated point on or forward of the nose or on or aft of the tail while maintaining a constant height and specified rate of movement around the point; apply controlled corrective action to maintain a constant rate of turn and to counter the effects of wind; adjust air transit ground speed to suit helicopter type, traffic conditions, congestion, and maintenance of control and to avoid collision with obstacles or other aircraft. For a helicopter with wheel landing gear, be able to do the following: select and maintain correct disk attitude and power required to initiate forwards movement of the helicopter on the surface; check and confirm the proper functioning of the wheel brake system; select and maintain correct disk attitude and power required to ground taxi and manoeuvre the helicopter on appropriate surfaces (wet and dry) at a safe speed in headwind, cross-wind and tailwind conditions; control the helicopter smoothly while ground taxiing and manoeuvring the helicopter with turns at a constant and safe rate of turn while maintaining an appropriate disk attitude and power setting; apply smooth and controlled actions to terminate at a nominated holding or parking point under different wind and surface conditions. **TR-SEH.2 – Conduct take-off to departure** Manage normal take-off to departure as follows: using approved technique and documented procedures perform a take-off, either from the ground or hover, and transition to forward flight and: complete appropriate checklists; perform a take-off safety briefing (this may be carried out prior to lift off to the hover if necessitated by location); ensure operating RPM within limits; clear the area, taxi into the take-off position; transition to forward flight and through translational lift using correct techniques; accelerate to and maintain the recommended or nominated climb speed using the correct profile: outside of the Height-Velocity (H-V) avoid curve; ensure obstacle avoidance; retract the landing gear after a positive rate of climb is established (if applicable); maintain correct power and attitude for the profile and IAS to be flown; comply with noise abatement procedures, where applicable; complete appropriate checks. Manage engine failure during take-off to departure as follows: self-brief, or brief crew members, stating a plan of action that will ensure the safest outcome in the event of an engine failure; maintain RRPM within the prescribed limits and control of the helicopter; perform autorotation to power termination or touchdown, as applicable; at the appropriate time, complete the engine failure shutdown checklist. **TR-SEH.3 – Control helicopter in normal flight**

Set power and maintain attitude to establish and maintain the following manoeuvres with the helicopter in balanced flight and trimmed (as applicable) within prescribed tolerances as follows:

straight and level: straight and level flight at normal cruise; maintains heading; maintains nominated altitude;

straight climbs and descents: maintain IAS for best angle of climb (VX); maintain IAS for best rate of climb (VY); maintain IAS for cruise climb; maintain IAS for cruise descent; maintain correct power setting as applicable to the rotorcraft; maintain heading;

turn onto specific headings (using magnetic compass) or geographical feature within the flight tolerances for the following: level turn; climbing turn, rate 1 or 20° bank; powered descending turn, 30° bank.

**TR-SEH.4 – Control helicopter during advanced manoeuvres** perform steep turns (45º) within the flight tolerances as follows: level turn altitude; exit on specified heading or geographical feature; perform autorotative flight: enter and maintain autorotative flight at nominated speed in balanced flight for the following profiles: descend at nominated heading and manufacturer’s recommended speed; conduct 180˚ autorotations using up to 45˚ angle of bank; autorotative flight at best range speed and minimum descent rate speed; maintain RRPM within limitations; perform landing or power termination as applicable; perform power termination: maintain RRPM within limitations; commence flare at appropriate height for the prevailing conditions and reduce ground speed and rate of descent; control attitude to achieve a decreasing closure rate and reducing rate of descent; control yaw, engine and RRPM; terminate the helicopter to a hover or hover taxi within tolerances of termination point without lateral or rearward drift; perform autorotative landing: commence flare at appropriate height for the prevailing conditions and reduces ground speed and rate of descent; control RRPM; select and maintain helicopter at the hover attitude without lateral or backward movement; control touchdown rate; control yaw; land helicopter with zero or minimum run-on speed within tolerances of nominated touchdown point without lateral or backward drift.

**TR-SEH.5 – Manage abnormal and emergency conditions** manage engine failure using the correct technique and applying the applicable checklists, procedures and planning during the following: hover and hover taxi; take-off and departure; cruise flight; approach and landing; manage control malfunction as follows: identify tail rotor malfunction during flight and take appropriate action following required checklists and procedures; select and manoeuvre helicopter to the safest landing area within area of regard; identify jammed primary controls, carry out manoeuvres to safely remediate the problem, and land at a suitable location for the following: jammed pedals; jammed or limited cyclic or collective; manage system malfunctions by identifying critical system malfunction during flight and take appropriate action following required checklists and procedures for: hydraulic system emergencies (if applicable); electrical system emergencies; clutch system emergencies (if applicable); engine governing system emergencies; perform recovery from the following (if applicable): vortex ring condition; loss of tail rotor effectiveness; low ‘g’ and mast bumping; control helicopter throughout, and manoeuvre the helicopter to the safest landing area available.

**TR-SEH.6 – Conduct a descent and arrival to an aerodrome** plan and conduct descent; join traffic pattern; maintain a safe separation from other traffic joining, departing or in the traffic pattern.

**TR-SEH.7 – Fly a full circuit pattern** perform a full circuit pattern (5 legs) within the tolerances specified for the relevant flight path; manage engine failure in the circuit: maintain control of the aircraft; perform recall actions correctly; select a suitable landing area within gliding distance, on the aerodrome or elsewhere; perform emergency procedures correctly and land the aircraft if the engine cannot be restarted; advise ATS or other agencies capable of providing assistance of situation and intentions; brief passengers about flight situation, brace position and harness security; land aircraft ensuring safest outcome if an engine restart is not achieved.

**TR-SEH.8 – Conduct a landing**

Perform the following while operating within the limitations prescribed in the RFM:

land on, and lift off from, sloping ground;

land, take off and manoeuvre in a confined area;

limited power approach and landing and take-off;

land and take-off from a pinnacle or ridgeline.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR; single-engine helicopter with dual controls, electronic intercom and dual control brakes, if fitted; aerodromes or HLS; sealed, gravel or grass surfaces; limitations, such as those imposed by local noise abatement procedures and curfews; operational hazards, which may include variable surfaces, loose objects, personnel, birds and propeller wash, rotor wash and jet blast; simulated abnormal and emergency situations; simulated hazardous weather.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: general aircraft data; make, type and model of helicopter, designation of engines, take-off and rated power; stated airspeed limitations including, but not limited to: VNE (at varying AUW and density altitudes) VH, configuration airspeed limits VLO, VTURB, maximum cross-wind; low speed wind limits; RRPM limits (Power ON and Power OFF); engine, transmission and any other stated limits in the RFM; slope landing limitations (if available); emergency procedures for the following: engine failure in the hover; taxiing; during transitions before and after take-off; in the cruise; on final approach before and after landing; engine fire on the ground and airborne; electrical fire on the ground and airborne; cabin fire in flight; N1, torque split indications; identify malfunctioning governor in flight and manage the related engine; corrective action to be taken when engine run-up or run-down has been diagnosed; the following weight and balance topics: weight, balance and performance; permissible take-off weight; maximum gross weight, landing weight, ramp weight and zero fuel weight; centre of gravity position for any specified conditions; centre of gravity limitations; appropriate charts to determine centre of gravity; calculated centre of gravity position and confirm it is within limits; the following take-off and landing topics: continuing and rejected take-off distances; take-off decision point; landing decision point; climb performance, hover out of ground effect and height–velocity diagram charts; failed engine operations; the following aircraft systems: fuel system; hydraulic system; electrical system; oil system; stability augmentation, AFCS and FDS (as applicable); anti-icing and de-icing systems (as applicable); heating and ventilation systems; pitot and static system; fire extinguisher system (as applicable); engine systems; transmission and rotor systems; display systems (as applicable); undercarriage system (fixed or retractable as applicable); the following key hazards including, for each, the typical causal factors and contributing operational situations, avoidance and recognition of symptoms and recovery techniques: vortex ring state; ground resonance; loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE); low ‘g’ and mast bumping; overpitching or low RRPM – rotor stall; retreating blade stall; recirculation; dynamic rollover.

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to operate a multi-engine helicopter.

Elements and performance criteria **TR-MEH.1 – Control helicopter on the ground** For all helicopters: prepare for start as follows: using an orderly procedure with checklists, inspect and prepare the helicopter, including those items recommended by the manufacturer, for a flight; Manage engine failure during take-off to departure as follows: self-brief, or brief crew members, stating a plan of action that will ensure the safest outcome in the event of an engine failure; maintain RRPM within the prescribed limits and control of the helicopter; correctly identify and confirm the failed engine(s) and at the appropriate time, complete the engine failure shutdown checklist for the following situations: engine failure prior to reaching take-off decision point: conduct the rejected take-off procedure in accordance with AFM and POH; apply the appropriate power within the AFM limits for the configuration being flown; perform a controlled landing in the rejected take-off distance available; engine failure after take-off: maintain control of the helicopter; set maximum contingency power on serviceable engine; accelerate to VTOSS (if applicable); identify and confirm failed engine; at the appropriate time, complete the engine failure shutdown checklist; climb multi-engine helicopter not below VYSE; land helicopter at nearest appropriate landing area. **TR-MEH.3 – Control helicopter in normal flight**

Set power and maintain attitude to establish and maintain the following manoeuvres with the helicopter in balanced flight and trimmed (as applicable) within prescribed tolerances as follows:

straight climbs and descents: maintain IAS for best angle of climb (VX); maintain IAS for best rate of climb (VY); maintain IAS for cruise climb; maintain IAS for cruise descent; maintain correct power setting as applicable to the rotorcraft; maintain heading;

land on, and lift off from, sloping ground;

land, take off and manoeuvre in a confined area;

limited power approach and landing and take-off;

land and take-off from a pinnacle or ridgeline (CPL).

FR-SEH Single-engine helicopter flight review

Unit description

This unit describes the standards required for a single-engine helicopter class rating and a single‑engine helicopter type rating flight review.

Elements and performance criteria **FR-SEHC.1 – Conduct flight** start, lift-off, hover and taxi helicopter ready for take-off; perform a normal take-off and departure; perform general handling manoeuvres, including the following: perform steep turns through at least 360°; conduct low flying at 500 ft AGL and perform a reversal turn; perform circuit rejoin and at least 1 full circuit pattern; perform a missed approach; perform hover, taxi, take-off, approach and landing in a cross-wind if conditions permit; conduct operations on sloping ground and in confined areas (where possible). **FR-SEAHC.2 – Manage aircraft systems** ensure sufficient fuel is loaded and fuel consumption is monitored and managed throughout the flight; manage the aircraft fuel system; manage all other aircraft systems. **FR-SEHC.3 – Navigation (optional)** plan flight of at least 3 legs and submit flight plan in accordance with AIP; conduct a departure; navigate en route using visual and instrument navigation systems; perform diversion procedure; demonstrate lost procedure; conduct arrival. **FR-SEHC.4 – Airspace** comply with airspace procedures and requirements; operate aircraft radio and conform to standard radio procedures. **FR-SEHC.5 – Instrument flying (optional)** perform basic flight manoeuvres using full instrument panel; recover from upset situations and unusual aircraft attitudes to straight and level flight; perform checks and monitor system for serviceability. **FR-SEHC.6 – Manage non-normal and emergency conditions** perform autorotation to touchdown or power termination; manage simulated engine failure during hover or hover taxi; manage aircraft system malfunctions other than engine failure; manage hydraulic system failure; perform recovery from the following (if applicable): vortex ring condition; loss of tail rotor effectiveness; low ‘g’ and mast bumping; manage loss of tail rotor control for the following: forward flight; hover. **FR-SEHC.7 – Non-technical skills** recognise and manage threats and errors during pre-flight planning and in-flight; maintain effective lookout and situational awareness; assess situations and make appropriate decisions; set priorities and manage tasks; maintain effective communication with stakeholders; communicate effectively using aeronautical radio. **FR-SEHC.8 – Manage passengers and cargo** conduct pre-flight and in-flight safety briefings to ensure passengers are familiar with safety procedures, emergency equipment, exits and operational requirements; manage cargo.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; simulated conditions can be used; for FR-SEH.5 – *instrument flying*, simulated or actual instrument conditions; for FR-SEH.6 – *manage non-normal and emergency conditions*, performance criteria are limited according to the type of aircraft being used.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: privileges, limitations and responsibilities of the licences, ratings and endorsements the applicant holds; flight review requirements; obtaining, interpreting and applying meteorological and aeronautical information; navigation and flight planning for day VFR operations; diversion and lost procedures; weight and balance and aircraft performance; operation of systems fitted to the aircraft that is used in the flight review; extracting and applying aircraft performance data for the aircraft that is used in the flight review; limitations applicable to the rotorcraft being flown for the flight review; airspace requirements and procedures; helicopter landing sites; manage cargo and passengers; hazard identification and risk management; low inertia characteristics; for each of the following, the typical causal factors and contributing operational situations, avoidance and recognition of symptoms and recovery techniques: vortex ring generation; ground resonance; loss of tail rotor effectiveness; low ‘g’ and mast bumping; overpitching/low RRPM – rotor stall; retreating blade stall; recirculation; dynamic rollover; non-normal and emergency procedures, including full and partial failures; local operating procedures; hazardous weather; airworthiness requirements; reporting requirements; ERSA normal and emergency procedures; current and recently changed legislation and procedures that are relevant to the applicant’s licences, ratings and endorsements.
