inspect mooring lines, bumpers, anchors, life jackets and rafts for condition and stowage when appropriate. **DFE8.3 – Operate amphibious aircraft during all phases of flight** operate single- or multi-engine floatplane or floating hull amphibious aircraft during all phases of normal and abnormal flight, on the water and the land, to the standards specified for a private or commercial pilot in this MOS for aeroplane class ratings; land amphibious aircraft on water with undercarriage retracted; land amphibious aircraft on land with undercarriage extended; extend undercarriage in water when transiting to land (beaching); retract undercarriage in water after taxiing from land to water; operate all amphibious aircraft systems, equipment and engines. **DFE8.4 – Manage abnormal or emergency situations in amphibious aircraft** identify and confirm abnormal or emergency situation; maintain control of aircraft; manage or rectify abnormal or emergency situation; perform abnormal and emergency actions when applicable; perform failed engine procedures in accordance with standards specified in class or type rating requirements.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR; cross-wind, headwind and tailwind to the limits of the aircraft; approved floating hull aircraft; salt and fresh waterways; variable sea states; confined waterways; variable marine traffic; maritime regulations and procedures; limitations, such as those imposed by local noise abatement procedures or curfews; simulated abnormal and emergency situations; simulated hazardous weather.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: differences between a seaplane, floatplane, flying boat (floating hull) and amphibious aircraft; aircraft performance with respect to: design features for seaplanes, floatplanes and floating hulls; and the differences between an aircraft that is fitted with the feature and the same type of aircraft that doesn’t have the feature; how to interpret Beaufort scale readings and ascertain wind velocity; how movement of the centre of buoyancy affects amphibious aircraft manoeuvrability on the water; how the centre of resistance to lateral motion affects the operation of an amphibious aircraft; why water rudders are not used for take-off; the type of undercarriage position indicators fitted to the aircraft, and the method of indicating undercarriage retracted; the method of emergency lowering of the undercarriage; how to extract information from maritime tide chart and determine the tide height and state at any specified place or time; how the centre of buoyancy can be varied when an amphibious aircraft is on the water; how movement of the centre of resistance affects amphibious aircraft manoeuvrability on the water; functions of a ventral fin on an amphibious aircraft; the function of float struts, spreader bars and bracing wires; requirements that apply to floats with regard to minimum number of water-tight compartments and capability of supporting the amphibious aircraft weight when compartments are flooded; method of detecting water inside a float and how to remove the water; function of the ‘step’ at the bottom of a float or hull; hazards associated with excessive swells.

DFE9 Helicopter float alighting gear

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to operate a helicopter fitted with float alighting gear on land and water.

Elements and performance criteria **DFE9.1 – Conduct pre-flight inspection of float alighting gear** conduct pre-flight inspection of helicopter and float alighting gear; confirm fitment, inflation, condition and security of float alighting gear; ensure removal of all aircraft locking devices. **DFE9.2 – Start and stop engine on water** perform all checklists and emergency procedures associated with starting and stopping an engine and rotors; perform free-floating start-up (as permitted by AFM or POH) and moored start-up and shutdown; start and stop engine and rotors correctly; identify abnormal or emergency situations on start or shutdown and manages correctly. **DFE9.3 – Taxi helicopter on water** manoeuvre helicopter without incident on water over a prescribed track while allowing for prevailing conditions; comply with approved marshalling signals. **DFE9.4 – Take-off helicopter from a solid surface and from water** perform pre-take-off checks and after-take-off checks correctly; perform take-off, transition and climb from a solid surface; perform take-off, transition and climb from water. **DFE9.5 – Operate helicopter fitted with float alighting gear in normal flight** operate helicopter fitted with float alighting gear in normal flight in accordance with standards for helicopter specified in this MOS; manage reduced aircraft performance in float configuration. **DFE9.6 – Land on float alighting gear on land and on water** identify aiming point, touchdown point and any alignment features; land helicopter without harshness onto a nominated touchdown point from hovering flight without longitudinal, lateral, yawing or rolling movements; ensure no aft movement when landing on water; ensure landing area on a solid surface is clear of protuberances and sharp objects; ensure helicopter is securely on the surface prior to fully lowering collective; perform after-landing checks; for a mishandled landing – implement a decision in the time available to initiate a mishandled landing to the hover when the landing standard cannot be achieved. **DFE9.7 – Manage abnormal or emergency actions in helicopter fitted with float alighting gear** identify abnormal or emergency situation; control helicopter; perform abnormal or emergency procedures correctly.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR in variable weather conditions; cross-wind, headwind and tailwind to the limits of the aircraft; approved helicopter fitted with float alighting gear; helicopter landing sites; salt and fresh waterways; variable sea states; confined waterways; variable marine traffic; maritime regulations and procedures; limitations, such as those imposed by local noise abatement procedures or curfews; simulated abnormal and emergency situations; simulated hazardous weather.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: maximum inflation pressure of the float alighting gear; maximum operating altitude permitted with float alighting gear fitted; maxim wave height permitted for float alighting gear operations in the helicopter type flown; how to calculate the maximum inflation pressure for the flotation devices; take-off distance required with the float configuration; the maximum wind speed for 360° pivot turns; hazards associated with a landing that is performed with a partially deflated float; avoidance measures for dynamic rollover; avoidance measures for ground resonance.

SECTION 5 OPERATIONAL RATING AND ENDORSEMENT STANDARDS

INSTRUMENT RATING

CIR Conduct an IFR flight

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct a flight in an aircraft under the IFR.

Elements and performance criteria **CIR.1 – Plan a flight under the IFR** determine aircraft is properly equipped and serviceable for IFR flight; possess and use all the required documentation that is current to plan an IFR flight; prepare an accurate flight plan that ensures all applicable operational requirements are met; make flight notification; check navigation system database is current; initialise navigation system (as applicable); conduct navigation system validity check (as applicable); conduct RAIM check if required; select, load, check and activate the flight plan (as applicable). **CIR.2 – Perform an instrument departure** prepare aircraft and aircraft systems for departure; demonstrate consideration of and planning for non-normal and emergencies during departure; demonstrate adequate knowledge of both of published and cleared and non‑published and non-cleared instrument departures; establish lowest take-off minima required considering aircraft performance, aerodrome, available instrument approaches and environmental conditions; conduct instrument departure to comply with obstacle clearance requirements. **CIR.3 – Conduct a published instrument departure (all engines)** perform a SID or other published departure; maintain assigned SID, including all tracks, headings, altitudes and speeds; perform a cleared departure safely and maintain tracks, headings, altitudes and speeds within specified tolerances. **CIR.4 – Conduct an instrument departure (1 engine inoperative) – simulated IMC** for single-engine aircraft instrument endorsements: following engine failure establish optimum flight path and manoeuvres aircraft towards most suitable terrain considering conditions; time permitting conduct checklists and radio calls. for multi-engine aircraft instrument endorsements: during departure manages aircraft following a simulated 1 engine inoperative event; maintain aircraft flight path within published tolerances; conduct checklists and radio calls; maintain terrain clearance; assess condition and decide to continue or return to aerodrome. **CIR.5 – Navigate aircraft under the IFR using ground-based and satellite-based navigational systems** demonstrate adequate knowledge of the published procedures associated with navigating an aircraft under the IFR using ground-based and satellite-based navigational systems; navigate aircraft under the IFR in accordance with published procedure using ground‑based and satellite-based navigational systems; position fix is determined with reference to navigation aid and systems using ground‑based and/or satellite-based navigational systems; tracks are intercepted to and from stations and way points with reference to navigation aids/systems using ground-based and satellite-based navigational systems; perform ground-based and satellite-based navigational systems confidence and integrity checks; requirement for an unplanned diversion is recognised and confirmed; route to alternate aerodrome, navigation aid and revised track is determined; planned route maintains height above the LSALT; flight planned route is diverted to track to alternate aerodrome, navigation aid or aerodrome; operational information for alternate aerodrome(s) is reviewed and applied according to published procedures; fuel plan is reviewed and amended according to published procedures; hazardous weather conditions are identified and avoided; procedures for penetration of hazardous weather are demonstrated and explained; aircraft systems are employed to mitigate the effects of hazardous weather; aircraft is configured to comply with turbulence penetration procedures; passenger and crew are restrained; procedures for penetrating turbulence are explained and demonstrated; identify and manage non-normal and emergency events. **CIR.6 – Perform a descent and arrival under the IFR** demonstrate adequate knowledge of the published procedures for the conduct of a descent and arrival to an aerodrome; perform a descent and published arrival procedure to an aerodrome. **CIR.7 – Perform a published holding procedure** demonstrate adequate knowledge of a published holding procedure; track aircraft to the holding fix and performs holding procedure (entry, full holding pattern and exit) safely. **CIR.8 – Perform an instrument approach 2D or 3D** demonstrate adequate knowledge of published procedures associated with an instrument approach; perform an instrument approach unique to the instrument approach type; maintain a stabilised flight path within specified tolerances during the approach procedure. **CIR.9 – Perform an instrument approach 1 engine inoperative (multi-engine aircraft only) – simulated IMC** at or before the FAF, identify, control and establish aircraft flight path within specified tolerances following an engine failure; complete checklists and radio calls; from the missed approach point conducts a missed approach whilst maintaining flight path within specified tolerances. **CIR.10 – Perform visual approach operations (includes visual circling where applicable)** demonstrate adequate knowledge of published procedures for the conduct of a visual approach; conduct a visual circling approach requiring at least a 90o change of heading to establish the aircraft onto the final approach leg to the specified runway whilst maintaining a stabilised flight path.

Range of variables element CIR.9 only applies to the multi-engine aeroplane, multi-engine helicopter and powered-lift aircraft instrument endorsements; for the single-engine aeroplane instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be a single-engine aeroplane; for the multi-engine aeroplane instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be a multi-engine aeroplane; for the single-engine helicopter instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be a single-engine helicopter; for the multi-engine helicopter instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be a multi-engine helicopter; for the powered-lift aircraft instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be a powered-lift aircraft; for the gyroplane instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be a gyroplane; for the airship instrument endorsement, the aircraft must be an airship; activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; IMC or Simulated IMC conditions; aircraft or approved synthetic training device; turbine or piston power plants; day and night; analogue or digital flight decks; autopilots and flight management systems; CTA and OCTA airspace; RVSM or non-RVSM airspace; AIP, Jeppesen or other approved IAL plates; approved checklists; FMS.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: full panel instrument manoeuvres; limited and partial panel instrument manoeuvres; AIP and published regulations; PBN procedures; approved aircraft flight manual; relevant sections of published regulations; airspace requirements and procedures under IFR conditions; IFR route planning requirements; use of the navigational computer; aircraft fuel planning, including holding, alternate, fixed reserve and usage rates; visual and instrument flight rules and procedures; factors affecting en route performance, range and endurance; critical point and point of no return; meteorological considerations for an IFR flight; icing conditions and hazards; requirements for an alternate aerodrome; determine take-off minima for single and twin engine aircraft at aerodromes with and without suitable departure or instrument approach procedures; conditions for take-off if a forecast cannot be obtained; departure procedures; transponder codes; when departure track must be established; contents of airborne and departure reports, and when these must be made; pilot's responsibility in an IFR visual departure; procedures for loss of radio communication; procedures for abnormal operations and emergencies; aerodrome and en route holding procedures;

(za) IFR cruising levels, selection and hazards;

(zb) operations, functions, modes, limitations and errors of navigations aids and systems;

(zc) instrument approach procedure chart;

(zd) instrument approach procedures and limitations, including the minimum system components required to conduct an approach;

(ze) correct sector entry join for entering the holding pattern of the approach procedure;

(zf) tracking tolerance and altitude limitations for flying a published arc of the approach procedure;

(zg) approach procedure applicable minima for aircraft;

(zh) conditions under which a circling approach must be discontinued and a missed approach initiated;

(zi) circling area applicable to the aircraft performance category being flown;

(zj) when an aircraft may descend below the MDA (day and night);

(zk) procedure to conduct a missed approach from any nominated point within a circling area on a specified approach;

(zl) read and interpret a STAR chart;

(zm) STAR procedures and limitations;

(zn) pilot's responsibilities when STAR clearance is given or cancelled;

(zo) applicable instrument approach procedure or visual approach at end of STAR;

(zp) knowledge of STAR radio procedures;

(zq) procedures for loss of radio communication during STAR;

(zr) procedures for abnormal operations and emergencies during STAR, including navigation aid failure;

(zs) conditions permitting descent below minima;

(zt) procedure for joining the circuit from an approach procedure;

(zu) approach procedure missed approach procedure;

(zv) minimum obstacle clearance criteria during an approach procedure missed approach procedure;

(zw) knowledge of approach procedure radio procedures;

(zx) procedures for loss of radio communication during an approach procedure;

(zy) procedures for abnormal operations and emergencies during an approach procedure, including navigation aid failure, loss of signal integrity and disparity between aids.

IAP2 Conduct an instrument approach 2D

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to perform a 2D instrument approach operation.

Elements and performance criteria **IAP2.1 – Prepares for approach** review latest available information for destination; conduct navigation system validity check (as applicable); conduct RAIM check if required; select, load, check and activate the flight plan (as applicable); select and brief current approach chart for the approach to be flown; check and confirm navigation aid required for the approach is serviceable. **IAP2.2 – Conducts initial approach** set altimeter QNH correctly; manoeuvre aircraft to the holding fix. **IAP2.3 – Conducts a holding pattern** from the holding fix enter and perform a holding pattern; fly aircraft in accordance with procedure. **IAP2.4 – Conducts an approach** update and set Altimeter QNH; use automation appropriately; approach performed correctly and within published tolerances; navigation aid signal integrity monitored during approach; from the final approach fix to minima aircraft is flown to a stabilised descent profile; after establishing visual reference, a visual circling or runway approach is conducted for a landing on the selected runway. **IAP2.5 – Conducts a missed approach** conditions requiring a missed approach are recognised and missed approach is initiated; aircraft is manoeuvred to MAPt; missed approach procedure is conducted in accordance with the IAL chart; obstacle clearance in IMC or simulated IMC is maintained.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; tasks may be undertaken in: IMC; VMC with simulated IMC conditions; performance may be demonstrated in: single-engine aircraft; multi-engine aircraft; approved flight simulation training device; variable air traffic conditions; variable weather conditions; variable flight situations; abnormal situations; differing classes of airspace; aircraft may include: fixed wing; helicopter; other commercial or military aircraft; crew may include: single pilot; multi-crew; instruments may be: fitted flight instruments suitable for instrument flight; head up display suitable for instrument flight; performance must be demonstrated using azimuth guidance and CDI guidance in the following: tracking; holding pattern; approach operations; missed approach operations; limitations may be imposed by: local noise abatement requirements and curfews; airspace endorsements; conditions may include: a method of simulating IMC; simulated icing conditions; moderate turbulence; simulated hazardous weather; autopilot and flight director; FMS and other NAV system; simulation of emergency and abnormal procedures; one of the following kinds of 2D instrument approach procedures: NDB; VOR and LOC; DGA (DME/GNSS Arrival); RNP-LNAV (RNAV/GNSS) and RNP-LP (WAAS required) approaches may include: NDB; VOR; DME or GNSS arrival procedure; RNP APCH LNAV and RNP APCH LP [charted as RNAV-(GNSS)]; LLZ; for an approach — NDB private instrument endorsement, competency must be demonstrated using a non-directional beacon navigation system; for an approach — VOR/LLZ private instrument endorsement, competency must be demonstrated using a VHF omni-range/localiser navigation system; for an approach — DME or GNSS private instrument endorsement, competency must be demonstrated using distance measuring equipment or a global navigation satellite system; for an approach — Approach – RNP APCH-2D private instrument endorsement, competency must be demonstrated using: a global navigation satellite system; or another kind of area navigation-based system.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: instrument approach procedures and limitations; sector entry join procedures for entering a holding pattern; tracking tolerance and altitude limitations for flying the published approach procedure; procedure for joining the circuit from an approach procedure; minimum obstacle clearance criteria during a approach procedure and missed approach procedure; missed approach procedure for an approach; radio procedures during an approach; loss of radio communication during an approach procedure; abnormal operations and emergencies procedures during an approach, including navigation aid failure; GNSS system fundamentals and principles of operations; requirements applicable to pilots and equipment for GNSS operations; cause and magnitude of typical GNSS errors; human factors limitations associated with the use of GNSS equipment; operating procedures which provide safeguards against GNSS navigational errors; GNSS operating procedures for navigation tasks; GNSS operational and serviceability checks; GNSS warnings and messages; tracking tolerances, automatic Way-point sequencing, CDI sensitivity and RAIM availability parameters for entry, RAIM availability and approach segments; mode of operation required during each segment of a GNSS/NPA; conditions required to transition to and operate in that mode of operation for the GNSS/NPA, and the associated CDI sensitivity and RAIM protection provided; parameters applicable to RAIM warnings in the en route, terminal and approach modes; effects of availability or otherwise of barometric altimeter-aiding on RAIM availability and prediction; effects of satellite unserviceability on the reliability of each type of prediction; effect of each type of RAIM prediction on operational requirements; prediction limitations that apply to availability of approach RAIM at the destination or alternate aerodrome; operational requirements which apply to planning a flight on the basis of conducting a RNAV (GNSS) procedure at the destination;

(za) factors that adversely affect the conduct of a GNSS/NPA, and suitable pilot procedures to minimise such effects;

(zb) operating procedures for GNSS equipment which reduce or eliminate errors.

IAP3 Conduct an instrument approach 3D

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to perform a 3D instrument approach procedure.

Elements and performance criteria **IAP3.1 – Prepares for approach** review latest available information for destination; conduct navigation system validity check (as applicable); conduct RAIM/SBAS check if required; select, load, check and activate the flight plan (as applicable); select and brief current approach chart for the approach to be flown; check and confirm navigation aid required for the approach is serviceable. **IAP3.2 – Conducts initial approach** set altimeter QNH; manoeuvre aircraft to the holding fix. **IAP3.3 – Conducts a holding pattern** from the holding fix enter and perform a holding pattern; fly aircraft in accordance with procedure. **IAP3.4 – Conducts an approach** update and set altimeter QNH; uses automation appropriately; navigation aid signal integrity monitored during approach; vertical and lateral path flown within published tolerances; specified altitude check on glide slope is performed; from the final approach fix to minima aircraft is flown to a stabilised descent profile; after establishing visual reference, a visual circling or runway approach is conducted for a landing on the selected runway. **IAP3.5 – Conducts a missed approach** conditions requiring a missed approach are recognised and missed approach is initiated; aircraft is manoeuvred to MAPt; missed approach procedure is conducted in accordance with the IAL chart; obstacle clearance in IMC or simulated IMC is maintained.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; tasks may be undertaken in: IMC; VMC with simulated IMC conditions; performance may be demonstrated in: single-engine aircraft; multi-engine aircraft; synthetic training device approved by the relevant authority; variable air traffic conditions; variable weather conditions; variable flight situations; abnormal situations; differing classes of airspace; aircraft may include: fixed wing; helicopter; other commercial or military aircraft; crew may include: single pilot; multi-crew; instruments may be: fitted flight instruments suitable for instrument flight; head up display suitable for instrument flight; limitations may be imposed by: local noise abatement requirements and curfews; airspace endorsements; conditions may include: a method of simulating IMC; simulated icing conditions; moderate turbulence; simulated hazardous weather; autopilot and flight director; FMS other NAV system; simulation of emergency and abnormal procedures; one of the following kinds of 3D instrument approach procedures: ILS and MLS and GLS; RNP-LNAV/VNAV (Baro) and RNP-LPV (WAAS required); Reserved for an approach — Approach – RNP APCH-3D private instrument endorsement, competency must be demonstrated using barometric-aided vertical guidance; for an approach — ILS private instrument endorsement, competency must be demonstrated using: an instrument landing system; or a microwave landing system; or a global navigation satellite system with ground-based augmentation.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: types of approach lighting systems; use of and precautions with approach slope indicators; low-visibility operations and environmental limitations (where applicable); contaminated runway operations; runway markings and lighting; temperature effects on altimeter; adjustment to Baro determined minima for temperature effect; automation and FMS management for low-visibility operations (where applicable); equipment redundancy during low-visibility operations (where applicable); RVR versus SVR.

PRIVATE IFR RATING

PIF Conduct a private instrument flight rules flight

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct of a Private IFR flight.

Elements and performance criteria **PIF.1 – Plan a flight under the IFR** determine aircraft is properly equipped and serviceable for IFR flight; initialise navigation system (as applicable); conduct navigation system validity check (as applicable); conduct RAIM/SBAS check if required; select, load, check and activate the flight plan (as applicable); use all the required documentation that is current to plan an IFR flight; prepare an accurate flight plan that ensures all applicable operational requirements are met; make flight notification; check navigation system database is current. **PIF.2 – Conduct a visual departure** conduct a visual departure until reaching the LSALT; ensure terrain clearance is maintained visually at all times during departure until reaching LSALT; for the night endorsement, comply with requirements for conducting a circling approach at night. **PIF.3 – En route IFR operation** use navigation systems to maintain en route navigation; perform en route procedures; comply with en route procedures in applicable types of airspace; ensures aircraft separation standards are maintained; recognise and confirm requirement for an unplanned diversion; determine route to alternate aerodrome, navigation aid and revised track; maintain height above the LSALT; divert from flight planned route to track to an alternate aerodrome, navigation aid or aerodrome; review and apply operational information for alternate aerodrome(s); review and amend fuel plan; identify and avoid hazardous weather conditions; demonstrate awareness of and take appropriate action in relation to penetration of hazardous weather; use aircraft systems effectively to mitigate the effects of hazardous weather; configure aircraft to comply with turbulence penetration procedures; identify and manage non-normal and emergency events. **PIF.4 – Navigating and holding using navigation system** operate navigation system; perform system confidence and integrity checks; use ground-based and satellite-based navigation systems to navigate aircraft under the IFR, including the following: fix position; intercept and maintain tracks to and from stations and way points; track aircraft to the holding fix and enter holding pattern; perform holding procedure (entry, full holding pattern and exit). **PIF.5 – Conduct instrument departure (if applicable)** conduct an instrument departure procedure to comply with obstacle clearance requirements; if applicable, perform SID or other published departure; maintain assigned SID, including tracks, headings, altitudes and speeds; comply with a departure clearance by maintaining tracks, headings, altitudes and speeds within specified tolerances; for single-engine aircraft instrument endorsements: following a simulated engine failure, establish optimum flight path and manoeuvre aircraft towards most suitable terrain considering conditions; time permitting, conduct checklists and radio calls; for multi-engine aircraft instrument endorsements: during departure manage aircraft following a simulated 1 engine inoperative event; maintain aircraft flight path; conduct checklists and radio calls; maintain terrain clearance; assess conditions and decide and then execute plan to continue or return to aerodrome. **PIF.6 – Perform an instrument approach operation (if applicable)** perform an instrument approach in accordance with procedures unique to the instrument approach type; maintain a stabilised flight path within specified tolerances during the approach operation; conduct a visual circling approach requiring at least a 90o change of heading to establish the aircraft onto the final approach leg to the specified runway whilst maintaining a stabilised flight path; for the night endorsement, comply with requirements for conducting a circling approach at night. **PIF.7 – Perform an instrument approach 1 engine inoperative (multi-engine aircraft only), if applicable** at or before the FAF identify, control and establish aircraft flight path within specified tolerances following an engine failure; complete checklists and radio calls; from the missed approach point conduct a missed approach whilst maintaining flight path within specified tolerances. **PIF.8 – Perform a descent, visual approach and landing** plan descent to establish VMC above or at the LSALT or MSA; maintain VMC during decent and arrival to the destination aerodrome; conduct visual approach and landing; for the night endorsement, comply with requirements for descending below LSALT at night.

activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; IMC or simulated IMC conditions; aircraft or approved synthetic training device; single-pilot or multi-crew aircraft; single-engine or multi-engine aircraft; NIGHT VFR RATING

NVR1 Conduct a traffic pattern at night

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to take off, land and operate an aircraft safely in the traffic pattern at night.

Elements and performance criteria **NVR1.1 – Control aircraft on the ground at night** instrument and cockpit lighting are adjusted to an appropriate level for taxiing; ATC instructions and manoeuvres of the aircraft on the ground at night within the approved movement area as defined by aerodrome ground lighting are complied with; aircraft lighting to identify obstructions, other aircraft and taxiway and runway limits is used as required; aircraft is taxied at a speed which allows for an adequate lookout to be maintained to avoid obstructions. **NVR1.2 – Activate pilot activated lighting (PAL)** appropriate radiotelephone frequency is utilised to activate PAL system when within radio range; transmit sequence is utilised to activate PAL system; wind indicator lighting is monitored to determine end of activation period. **NVR1.3 – Take-off aircraft at night** For aircraft in the aeroplane category, as follows: aircraft is lined up correctly in centre of runway in take-off direction; line-up checks appropriate to night take-off are completed; take-off by reference to flare path and runway lighting and aircraft instruments is executed; aircraft is rotated at manufacturer’s recommended speed; climb attitude and control aircraft in climb, after take-off solely by reference to instruments is completed; alignment with runway by visual reference and lookout is established and maintained; after take-off, checks are performed at a safe height. For aircraft in the helicopter category, as follows: accelerates helicopter in take-off direction on a prescribed track; recognises and controls translational lift; executes take-off by reference to flare path and runway lighting or HLS lighting and aircraft instruments; applies climb power and adjusts attitude to maintain climb speed appropriate to obstacle clearance requirements; aligns helicopter landing gear with the planned take-off direction until the point at which balanced flight is required; maintains helicopter outside the height-velocity chart avoid area; retracts undercarriage at a safe height and airspeed, if applicable; trims helicopter, if applicable; balances helicopter; performs after-take-off checks in accordance with approved checklist. **NVR1.4 – Fly a circuit pattern at night**

Performs a circuit pattern safely and in accordance with the specified procedures and approved techniques.

**NVR1.5 – Manage emergency situations at night** (in simulated conditions) aircraft control is maintained; emergency situation is managed in accordance published procedures; electrical lighting and power sources are monitored; electrical lighting and power source emergency procedures are conducted as appropriate.

**NVR1.6 – Perform a go-around** the need to conduct a go-around is recognised; go-around is performed from any point on base and final approach legs.

**NVR1.7 – Land at night, with and without the use of aircraft landing lights** circuit entry and pattern are performed with reference to runway environment; safe altitude is maintained by reference to aircraft instruments and runway lighting; aircraft is safely landed at night with and without landing lights; after landing checks are performed.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; for the single-engine aeroplane night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a single-engine aeroplane; for the multi-engine aeroplane night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a multi-engine aeroplane; for the helicopter night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a helicopter; for the powered-lift aircraft night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a powered-lift aircraft; for the gyroplane night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a gyroplane; for the airship night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a airship; night or simulated night conditions; aircraft or approved synthetic training device; analogue or digital flight decks; autopilots and flight management systems.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.7 of this MOS, night VFR rating; colour and pattern of the following: permanent threshold light; runway threshold identifications lights; displaced threshold lighting; runway edge lighting; runway end lighting; runway centreline lighting; obstacle lighting; method of activating PAL; method of activating Aerodrome Frequency Response Unit (AFRU) with PAL options; time that PAL remains illuminated; PAL warning for users that the lights are about to extinguish; operation and use of a VASI system; operation and use of a PAP) system; vestibular systems, namely the semicircular canals and otoliths, in helping the pilot maintain orientation; circumstances aggravate vestibular disorientation, and how to overcome this problem; causes that may aggravate, vestibular disorientation such as somatogravic illusions, somatogyral illusions and ‘graveyard spiral’, coriolis effect, and ‘leans’; conditions and causes under which visual illusions, such as ‘false horizons’, visual-cue illusions, relative motion illusions, ‘flicker effect’, ‘black hole’ illusion, and autokinesis may occur.

NVR2 Night VFR – single-engine aircraft

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct a NVFR operation in a single‑engine aircraft.

Elements and performance criteria **NVR2.1 – Determine aircraft meets requirements for NVFR flight** aircraft requirements for NVFR flight are determined; flight and navigation instruments, minimum electrical lighting and navigation equipment and any other requirements which are fitted to the aircraft are checked to ensure they are suitable and serviceable for NVFR flight. **NVR2.2 – Obtain and use current operational documents** operational documents applicable to the flight are obtained and checked for currency; applicable information contained in documents for flight planning and management is interpreted and applied; documents required for the flight are stowed and accessibility for the pilot during flight is ensured. **NVR2.3 – Prepare flight plan for NVFR flight** charts suitable for intended NVFR flight are selected and prepared; applicable information to prepare a flight plan which details tracks, distances, times, altitudes to be flown and fuel requirements to reach destination are obtained, analysed and applied; meteorological, airways facilities, aerodrome and NOTAM information applicable to planning and conducting a flight is obtained, interpreted and applied; routes to optimise options in the event of an engine failure are planned. **NVR2.4 – Determine operational requirements** suitability of the aerodrome lighting for night operations is determined; curfew requirements are complied with; duration of flight is determined; holding, alternate and reserve fuel requirements due to weather, navigation aid availability and aerodrome lighting are determined in accordance with operational requirements; total fuel requirements are calculated. **NVR2.5 – Make flight notification** flight notification is prepared for planned NVFR flight; completed flight notification is submitted; flight notification acceptance is confirmed. **NVR2.6 – Program navigation system** prepare data for transfer to approved airborne navigation system; navigation data is loaded and checked. **NVR2.7 – Select, operate and monitor navigation aids and systems** appropriate navigation aids and systems for the planned NVFR flight are selected and operated in accordance navigation aid and system requirements; integrity of navigation aid and systems information is monitored and maintained. **NVR2.8 – Make visual departure at night** obstacle clearance is ensured until reaching LSALT; departure track is intercepted within 5 nm of aerodrome conduct take-off and departure from an aerodrome which is remote from ground lighting as follows: climb out after take-off, using instruments as the primary reference; after take-off checks are performed at a safe height. **NVR2.9 – Navigate the aircraft under NVFR** cockpit and instrument lighting are adjusted to allow reference to documentation, instruments and lookout; manages and interprets outputs of on-board navigation systems; aircraft position fix is determined visually or with reference to navigation aid and system; updates navigation log; maintains fuel log; uses a recognised navigation work cycle; tracks are intercepted to and from visually or with reference to navigation aids and systems; track is maintained within tolerances specified in published procedures; timings are recorded, assessed and revised as required; station passage is recognised; planned route above LSALT is maintained; route and destination weather conditions are monitored and appropriate actions are executed; descent point is calculated and amended. **NVR2.10 – Comply with air traffic control rules and procedures for NVFR flights** separation from other air traffic maintained; airspace requirements are complied with; two-way communication is maintained with ATS and other aircraft; ATC clearances and radar vectoring instructions are complied with. **NVR2.11 – Manage hazardous weather conditions** hazardous weather conditions are identified and avoided; procedures for avoidance of hazardous weather are demonstrated and explained; aircraft systems are employed to mitigate the effects of hazardous weather. **NVR2.12 – Manage emergency situations at night** (in simulated conditions) aircraft control is maintained; emergency situation is managed in accordance published procedures; electrical lighting and power sources are monitored; electrical lighting and power source emergency procedures are conducted as appropriate. **NVR2.13 – Conduct a diversion to revised route or alternate aerodrome at night** requirement for an unplanned diversion is recognised and confirmed; route to alternate aerodrome, navigation aid and revised track is determined; planned route maintains height above LSALT in accordance with regulations while flying under NVFR; flight planned route is diverted to track to an alternate aerodrome, navigation aid or aerodrome; operational information for alternate aerodrome(s) is reviewed and applied according to published procedures; fuel plan is reviewed and amended according to published procedures. **NVR2.14 – Make visual approach at night** descent below LSALT is conducted in accordance with published procedures; track is maintained to destination aerodrome; conduct an approach and landing at an aerodrome that is remote from extensive ground lighting. **NVR2.15 – Perform a go-around** the need to conduct a go-around is recognised; go-around is performed from any point on base and final approach legs.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; tasks may be undertaken in NVFR conditions; performance may be demonstrated in the following as applicable: single-engine aircraft; synthetic training device approved by the appropriate authority; aircraft may include: fixed wing; helicopter; instruments may be: fitted flight instruments suitable for NVFR flight; head up display suitable for NVFR flight; limitations may be imposed by: local noise abatement requirements and curfews; airspace endorsements; Aircraft requirements may include: instruments; communication; navigation system; lighting; for the single-engine aeroplane night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a single-engine aeroplane; for the helicopter night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a helicopter; for the powered-lift aircraft night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a powered-lift aircraft; for the gyroplane night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a gyroplane; for the airship night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a airship.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.7 of this MOS, night VFR rating; navigation requirements for the following: a night visual flight using radio navigation systems; a night visual flight using self-contained or long-range navigation systems; a night visual flight using visual reference to ground and water; navigation tolerance for a night visual flight avoiding CTA; requirements for the following: positive radio fixing; the most precise track guidance; navigation requirements for night visual flight with respect to time interval between fixes, accuracy of time reference, and accuracy and procedures in track-keeping; procedures for night visual flight in all classes of airspace when diverting from track due to navigation or weather; route for night visual flight with respect to forecast weather, controlled airspace, prohibited, restricted and danger areas, engine out performance for multi-engine aircraft, specified route limitations, airways operational requirements, and availability of published routes, en route alternate aerodromes, navigation aids, rated coverage and radio communication; compulsory reporting points; route, aircraft equipment and navigation requirements for NVFR; LSALT for a night visual flight for a route published on a chart; dimensions of the significant safety sector when calculating LSALT for a route not published on a chart; methods of calculating LSALT for a route not published on a chart; calculation of LSALT when uncertain of position; conditions for descent below LSALT; pre-flight altimeter accuracy check for a night visual flight; altimetry procedures to all stages of a night visual flight operating at aerodromes where surrounding light is limited.

NVR3 Night VFR – multi-engine aircraft

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct a flight at night under the NVFR in a multi-engine aircraft.

Elements and performance criteria **NVR3.1 – Determine aircraft meets requirements for NVFR flight** aircraft requirements for NVFR flight are determined; flight and navigation instruments, minimum electrical lighting and navigation equipment and any other requirements which are fitted to the aircraft are checked to ensure they are suitable and serviceable for NVFR flight. **NVR3.2 – Obtain and use current operational documents** operational documents applicable to the flight are obtained and checked for currency; applicable information contained in documents for flight planning and management is interpreted and applied; documents required for the flight are stowed and accessibility for the pilot during flight is ensured. **NVR3.3 – Prepare flight plan for NVFR flight** charts suitable for intended NVFR flight are selected and prepared; calculates LSALT for planned flight using WAC; applicable information to prepare a flight plan which details tracks, distances, times, altitudes to be flown and fuel requirements to reach destination are obtained, analysed and applied; meteorological, airways facilities, aerodrome and NOTAM information applicable to planning and conducting a flight is obtained, interpreted and applied; routes to optimise options in the event of an engine failure are planned. **NVR3.4 – Determine operational requirements** suitability of the aerodrome lighting for night operations is determined; curfew requirements are complied with; duration of flight is determined; holding, alternate and reserve fuel requirements due to weather, navigation aid availability and aerodrome lighting are determined in accordance with operational requirements; total fuel requirements are calculated; calculates performance available and plans actions in the event of engine failure after take‑off; calculates performance available in the event of engine failure during cruise and determines if aircraft can maintain at least the LSALT for planned route until established within 3 nm of destination aerodrome with the runway in sight; replans if OEI performance indicates inability to maintain LSALT on planned route. **NVR3.5 – Make flight notifications** flight notification is prepared for planned NVFR flight; completed flight notification is submitted; flight notification acceptance is confirmed. **NVR3.6 – Program navigation system** prepare data for transfer to approved airborne navigation system; navigation data is loaded and checked. **NVR3.7 – Select, operate and monitor navigation aids and systems** appropriate navigation aids/systems for the planned NVFR flight are selected and operated in accordance navigation aid/system requirements; integrity of navigation aid/systems information is monitored and maintained. **NVR3.8 – Take-off at night at other than departure aerodrome which is remote from ground lighting** aircraft is lined up correctly in centre of runway in take-off direction; line-up checks appropriate to night take-off are completed; take-off by reference to flare path/runway lighting and aircraft instruments is executed; aircraft is rotated at manufacturer’s recommended speed; climb attitude and control aircraft in climb, after take-off solely by reference to instruments is completed; alignment with runway by visual reference and lookout is established and maintained; after take-off, checks are performed at a safe height. **NVR3.9 – Engine failure after take-off (performed in day VFR conditions)**

Under simulated IMC at a height not below 400 ft AGL controls aircraft following a simulated engine failure after take-off from the point of failure, carries out published engine failure procedures and establishes the aircraft at circuit height within prescribed tolerances for altitude and heading.

**NVR3.10 – Make a visual departure at night** obstacle clearance is ensured until reaching LSALT; departure track is intercepted within 5 nm of aerodrome.

**NVR3.11 – Navigate the aircraft in NVFR** cockpit and instrument lighting are adjusted to allow reference to documentation, instruments and lookout; manages and interprets outputs of on-board navigation systems; aircraft position fix is determined visually or with reference to navigation aid and system; updates navigation log; maintains fuel log; uses a recognised navigation work cycle; tracks are intercepted to and from visually or with reference to navigation aids and systems; track is maintained within tolerances specified in published procedures; timings are recorded, assessed and revised as required; station passage is recognised; planned route above LSALT is maintained; route and destination weather conditions are monitored and appropriate actions are executed; descent point is calculated and amended.

**NVR3.12 – Engine failure during cruise (not below LSALT at night)** following a simulated engine failure during cruise, carries out published engine failure‑procedures and establishes aircraft at a nominated altitude above LSALT for route within prescribed tolerances for altitude, track and heading; using a structured method develops and decides on a course of action to minimise threats for continuation of flight with 1 engine inoperative.

**NVR3.13 – Comply with air traffic control rules and procedures for NVFR flights** separation from other air traffic maintained; airspace requirements are complied with; two-way communication is maintained with ATS and other aircraft; ATC clearances and radar vectoring instructions are complied with.

**NVR3.14 – Manage hazardous weather conditions** hazardous weather conditions are identified and avoided; procedures for avoidance of hazardous weather are demonstrated and explained; aircraft systems are employed to mitigate the effects of hazardous weather.

**NVR3.15 – Manage emergency situations at night** (in simulated conditions) aircraft control is maintained; emergency situation is managed in accordance published procedures; electrical lighting and power sources are monitored; electrical lighting and power source emergency procedures are conducted as appropriate.

**NVR3.16 – Conduct a diversion to revised route or alternate aerodrome at night** requirement for an unplanned diversion is recognised and confirmed; route to alternate aerodrome, navigation aid and revised track is determined; planned route maintains height above LSALT in accordance with regulations while flying under NVFR; flight planned route is diverted to track to an alternate aerodrome, navigation aid or aerodrome; operational information for alternate aerodrome(s) is reviewed and applied according to published procedures; fuel plan is reviewed and amended according to published procedures.

**NVR3.17 – Make visual approach at night** descent below LSALT is conducted in accordance published procedures; track is maintained to destination aerodrome; with 1 engine inoperative, under day VFR conditions conducts a descent, circuit join, approach and landing from 3 nm at or above a simulated LSALT with 1 engine inoperative whilst maintaining prescribed flight tolerances.

**NVR3.18 – Land at night, with and without the use of aircraft landing lights at other than departure aerodrome which is remote from ground lighting** circuit entry and pattern are performed with reference to runway environment; safe altitude is maintain by reference to aircraft instruments and runway lighting; aircraft is safely landed at night with and without landing lights; after landing checks are performed.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; tasks may be undertaken in NVFR conditions; performance may be demonstrated in a: multi-engine aircraft; synthetic training device approved by the appropriate authority; aircraft may include: fixed wing; helicopter; crew may include: single pilot; multi-crew; instruments may be: fitted flight instruments suitable for NVFR flight; head up display suitable for NVFR flight; limitations may be imposed by: local noise abatement requirements and curfews; airspace endorsements; aircraft requirements may include: instruments; communication; navigation system; lighting; for the multi-engine aeroplane night VFR endorsement, the aircraft must be a multi-engine aeroplane.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.7, Night VFR rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; navigation requirements for the following: a night visual flight using radio navigation systems; a night visual flight using self-contained or long‑range navigation systems; a night visual flight using visual reference to ground and water; navigation tolerance for a night visual flight avoiding CTA; requirements for the following: positive radio fixing; the most precise track guidance; navigation requirements for night visual flight with respect to time interval between fixes, accuracy of time reference, and accuracy and procedures in track-keeping; procedures of night visual flight in all classes of airspace when diverting from track due to navigation or weather; route for night visual flight with respect to forecast weather, controlled airspace, prohibited, restricted and danger areas, engine out performance for multi-engine aircraft, specified route limitations, airways operational requirements, and availability of published routes, en route alternate aerodromes, navigation aids, rated coverage and radio communication; compulsory reporting points; route, aircraft equipment and navigation requirements for NVFR; LSALT for a night visual flight for a route published on a chart; dimensions of the significant safety sector when calculating LSALT for a route not published on a chart; methods of calculating LSALT for a route not published on a chart; calculation of LSALT when uncertain of position; conditions for descent below LSALT; pre-flight altimeter accuracy check for a night visual flight; altimetry procedures to all stages of a night visual flight;

NIGHT VISION IMAGING SYSTEM RATING

NVI Night vision imaging system operation

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to plan and conduct helicopter operations using night vision imaging systems (NVIS) at night.

Elements and performance criteria **NV1.1 – Plan NVIS operations** identifies task requirements and any hazards or risks; plans navigation and operational requirements; manual, including: NVFR or IFR operations; operational requirements and procedures; risk and hazard mitigation; contingency procedures; determine serviceability of NVG equipment and aircraft: determines helicopter certification MEL requirements for conducting an NVIS operation; inspects and ensures serviceability of NVG equipment; inspects and ensures serviceability and suitability of aircraft and aircraft lighting system for NVG operations; brief and de-brief NVG operations: pre-flight brief; briefs all stakeholders, including: a plan for recovery from inadvertent IMC entry and loss of visual cues, when appropriate; the transit flight, let-down and approach procedures; landing and take-off procedures; role functions and procedures; contingency management; post-flight brief; analyses objectives and outcomes of the flight and reviews operating procedures; analyses effectiveness and efficiency in the use and performance of role equipment; identifies achievements and any faults or errors that occurred during the NVG flight and provides guidance and feedback to crew members; ensures inspection, servicing and stowage arrangements for NVG equipment. **NV1.2 – Perform circuit procedures using NVG** performs hover, taxi, take-off, circuits and landing using NVG to the standards for night visual flight specified in this MOS; performs baulked landing procedures using NVG; performs cockpit procedures and checks during goggled and de‑goggled flight; take off and transit to and from area of operation using NVG; performs hover, taxi, take-off and transit to and from area of operations using NVG in accordance with NVFR standards specified in this MOS; descends aircraft to unlit HLS while avoiding terrain and obstructions using NVG; maintains control of aircraft during transition to and from goggled and de-goggled flight; identifies the unlit HLS and any obstructions or terrain using NVG; approach, land on, take-off from and climb out from an unlit HLS using NVG; approach and landing manoeuvres aircraft using instrument scan and visual cues; intercepts and maintains glide slope; identifies and confirms touchdown point and reference markers; approaches at a constant angle; terminates approach and establishes stable hover over HLS; lands helicopter on HLS using NVG, including: sloping ground landing; pinnacle and ridgeline landing; take-off and climb-out identifies obstructions and hazards using NVG; establishes stable hover; takes off helicopter, including: sloping ground take-off; pinnacle and ridgeline take-off; climbs helicopter steeply after take-off; avoids obstacles and terrain; establishes climb to LSALT. **NV1.3 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations using NVG** controls helicopter; identifies and confirms abnormal or emergency situations during aided flight; manages abnormal or emergency situation; manages inadvertent entry into IMC and re-establishment of VMC: manages loss of visual cues on take-off and landing during operations devoid of surrounding cultural lighting. **NV1.4 – Conduct NVIS operation** perform role functions; manage flight during multi-crew NVG operations: ensures that all crew members have role clarity and relevant information to achieve goals; ensures clear communications using standard operating procedures in accordance with Company Operations Manual; manages changing priorities and, if necessary, re-focuses crew members to accommodate the changed priorities; corrects individual or crew member deviations from standards; threat and error management: identifies environmental or operational threats that could affect the safety of the flight; develops options to mitigate or control threats; applies checklists and standard operating procedures to prevent aircraft handling, procedural or communication errors, and identifies committed errors before safety is affected or aircraft enters an undesired aircraft state; recognises undesired aircraft state; manipulates aircraft controls or systems, or modifies actions or procedures, to correct undesired aircraft state in the time available.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; for the class 1 endorsement, IFR where applicable; for the class 2 endorsement, NVFR conditions; goggled and de-goggled flight; approved aircraft fitted with flight instruments, including attitude and stabilised heading indicators with lighting adapted to NVG standards; operations without visible horizon; simulated hazardous weather; simulated abnormal and emergency situations; lit and unlit HLS.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.6, Night vision imaging system (NVIS) rating of Schedule 3 of this MOS; NVG equipment; human and aeromedical factors; NVG environment; terrain interpretation and navigation; NVG regulations; NVG flight planning; crew coordination; dangers of non-NVG-trained personnel and non-compatible lighting at landing sites.

LOW-LEVEL RATING

LL-A Aeroplane low-level operations

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to safely conduct low-level operations in aeroplanes.

Elements and performance criteria **LL-A.1 – Plan low-level operations** identify hazards, evaluate and manage risks at low level; complete consultation with all stake holders involved in the low-level operation to confirm task requirements; ensure aeroplane type and performance capability is appropriate for the task; assess and allow for the effects of fatigue and physical health on pilot performance; analyse and apply actual and forecast weather conditions to low-level operations; identify area of operations using chart and geographical features; assess geographical characteristics of the area of flying operations to ensure safe completion of the task; confirm location of ground support personnel when available; conduct appropriate reconnaissance and pre-manoeuvre or other relevant checks prior to descending below 500 ft AGL. **LL-A.2 – Flight component** correctly performs pre-flight inspection and determine aircraft serviceability for intended flight; initialises and checks data validity of area navigation system (if fitted); correctly operates aircraft; correctly performs take-off. **LL-A.3 – Aircraft handling** For this element, manoeuvres are performed at an altitude above 3,000 ft AGL for training purposes: perform level flight, climbing and descending turns up to 60° angle of bank (45° for multi‑engine aircraft): visual references utilised; speed monitored; bank attitude maintained; pitch attitude adjusted for bank angle; desired altitude maintained; rollout and level off anticipated; perform approach and recovery to the stall in level flight: recognise approach to stall conditions; maintain references by visual cues; identify the approach to stall; recover by AOA reduction and power application to minimise height loss; reconfigure aeroplane; perform approach to the stall in turning flight and recovers: recognise approach to stall conditions; maintain references by visual cues; identify the approach to stall; recover by AOA reduction and power application to minimise height loss; reconfigures aeroplane; recover from wing drop at the stall to straight and level in various configurations (limited to single‑engine aeroplanes): identify the approach to stall; recognise wing drop at the stall; reduce angle of attack to unstall the wing; prevent yaw; use available power and height to increase the aircraft energy state; avoid secondary stall; re-establish desired flight path and aircraft control with balanced control application; reconfigure aeroplane as required; perform maximum rate turning: apply maximum performance turning criteria; maximum power applied; maximum bank applied for turning performance commensurate with speed; maximum permitted ‘g’ applied commensurate with speed; achieve turning at maximum AOA; ensure aeroplane does not stall or exceed permitted G limits; release ‘g’ force during roll out of turn; perform minimum radius turning: apply minimum radius turning criteria; maximum power applied; height as low as safely practical; recognise stall warning indications (at the approach to the stall); ensure aeroplane does not stall; release ‘g’ force immediately prior to rolling out of the turn; manage the energy state of the aircraft: identify high kinetic energy situations; identify low kinetic energy situations; identify high potential energy situations; identify low potential energy situations; perform a forced landing following a simulated engine failure (single-engine aircraft only). **LL-A.4 – Low-level handling** For this element, manoeuvres are performed, manoeuvres are performed at an altitude of below 500 ft AGL but not below 100 ft AGL: manage the aircraft energy state; identify wind velocity; perform straight flight: adjust height according to terrain to maintain assigned height above ground level; recognise and manage the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; compensate for drift; perform turning at various bank angles up to 60° angle of bank at normal cruise speed: perform lookout; adjust power as required; manage the effects of flying over featureless terrain or water; recognise and manages the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; compensate for the effect of gradient wind; anticipate rollout; conduct procedure turns from a fixed ground reference point and compensate for the effect of gradient wind; demonstrate knowledge of the effect of false horizons; recognise and manage impact of sun glare on increased risk of collision with obstacles; demonstrate use of escape routes and rising ground; demonstrate flight at various speed and configurations not below the calculated stall speed +15 KIAS or safe single-engine speed +15 KIAS (for multi-engine aeroplanes); identify and maintain safe distance from pole stay wires; operate adjacent to powerlines and wires; identify the requirement to operate in the vicinity of powerlines and wires and assess risk; demonstrate awareness of wind effect in the vicinity of obstructions, mountainous terrain and illusions; identify poles, cross trees, wires and insulators to assist powerline and wire location; recognise and control the illusion of slipping and skidding during turns close to the ground; recognise the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; comply with airspace requirements and procedures; demonstrate correct navigation techniques and procedures at low level; navigate to a predetermined destination at a height below 500 ft AGL; correctly performs low level circuit and landing. **LL-A.6 – Execute forced landing (simulated) from below 500 ft AGL (single-engine aeroplane only)** identify potential forced-landing areas prior to and during low-level operations; recognise engine failure or any other emergency requiring a forced landing and conduct recall actions; maintain control of the aircraft – select the most appropriate landing area within gliding distance while avoiding any powerlines or obstructions; manoeuvre the aircraft to a landing area that achieves the safest outcome; explain plan of action and the landing techniques that would ensure the safest outcome when committed to a forced landing on unfavourable terrain or water. **LL-A.7 – Execute engine failure (simulated) from below 500 ft AGL (multi-engine aeroplane only)** identify potential escape routes prior to and during low-level operations; recognise engine failure or any other emergency and conduct recall actions; maintain control of the aeroplane; initiate climb to safe altitude; manoeuvre the aeroplane via escape route to a safe altitude; complete check system items; explain plan of action. **LL-A.8 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the aeroplane at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR in variable weather conditions; alternate landing areas; obstructions and vertical terrain; up to and including light turbulence; simulated emergency and abnormal situations; simulated hazardous weather; multi-engine and single-engine aeroplanes; winds in excess of 10 kts.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.5, Low-level rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; minimum height for flight by an aircraft over a city, town or populous area; legislative restrictions applicable to low flying; minimum lateral and vertical distances that an aircraft must avoid persons, vessels, vehicles, structures or livestock over a sparsely populated area; dangers associated with ‘out of balance’ flight manoeuvres when flying at low level; maximum rate turns and minimum radius turn criteria; aeroplane limitations; how unintended spinning may be induced.

LL-H Helicopter low-level operations

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to safely conduct low-level operations in helicopters.

Elements and performance criteria **LL-H.1 – Plan low-level operations** identify, evaluate and manage risks at low level; complete consultation with all stake holders involved in the low-level operation to confirm task requirements; ensure aircraft type and performance is appropriate for the task; assess and allow for the effects of fatigue and physical health on pilot performance; analyse and apply actual and forecast weather conditions to low-level operations; identify area of operations using chart and geographical features; assess geographical characteristics of the area of flying operations to ensure safe completion of the task; identify and avoid all obstructions; identify and avoid buildings, personnel, vehicles, animals, vegetation and nuisance areas. **LL-H.2 – Flight component** correctly perform pre-flight inspection and determine aircraft serviceability for intended flight; initialise and check data validity of area navigation system (if fitted); correctly operate aircraft; correctly perform take-off. **LL-H.3 – Aircraft handling (at an altitude above 1,500 ft AGL)** conduct pre-manoeuvre checks for each manoeuvre; demonstrate level flight, climbing and descending turns up to 60° angle of bank as follows: visual references utilised; speed monitored; bank attitude maintained; pitch attitude adjusted for bank angle; desired altitude maintained; rollout and level off anticipated; recognise the approach and demonstrate the recovery to retreating blade stall in level flight as follows: configure aircraft appropriately; recognise approach to retreating blade stall conditions; maintain references by visual cues; recover by reduction of collective (AOA) (consistent with available height and power application); recognise the approach and demonstrate the recovery to retreating blade stall in turning flight as follows: configure aircraft appropriately; recognise approach to retreating blade stall conditions; maintain references by visual cues; recover by AOA reduction (consistent with available height and power application); apply correct techniques for upset recovery in various configurations as follows: configure aircraft appropriately; recognise upset condition; maintain references by visual cues; recover to level flight condition; Reserved Reserved manage the energy state of the aircraft for the following: identify high kinetic energy situations; identify low kinetic energy situations; identify high potential energy situations; identify low potential energy situations. **LL-H.4 – Low-level handling (at an altitude of 200 ft AGL but not below 5 ft AGL)** manage the aircraft energy state; perform straight flight as follows: adjust height according to terrain to maintain assigned height above ground level; recognise and manage the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; compensate for drift; perform turning at various bank angles up to 60° angle of bank at normal cruise speed as follows: adjust power as required; recognise and manage the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; compensate for the effect of gradient wind; anticipate rollout; demonstrate use of escape routes and rising ground; demonstrate flight at various speed and configurations not below (safe single-engine speed +15 KIAS for multi-engine aircraft); operate adjacent to powerlines and wires; demonstrate awareness of wind effect in the vicinity of obstructions, mountainous terrain and illusions; recognise and control the illusion of slipping and skidding during turns close to the ground; recognise the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; maintain a constant altitude over featureless terrain or water; conduct procedure turns from a fixed ground reference point; demonstrate knowledge of the effect of false horizons; recognise and manage impact of sun glare on increased risk of collision with obstacles; identify escape routes and rising ground; identify the requirement to operate in the vicinity of powerlines and wires and assesses risk; identify and avoid powerlines (wires) by a minimum of 15 ft when crossing overhead; identify and avoid all powerlines and wires; identify poles, cross trees, wires and insulators to assist powerline and wire location; identify and avoid pole stay wires; perform quick stop manoeuvres; into wind and downwind entry as follows: identify termination point; decelerate helicopter; balance helicopter and maintain direction and altitude; maintain helicopter outside height velocity diagram requirements; hover over the termination point; perform quick stop manoeuvres, downwind entry; identify termination point; turn 180° by controlled corrective action (downwind entry); turn helicopter into wind and initiate deceleration; balance helicopter and maintain direction and altitude; perform flight at various speed and configurations; identify and maintain safe distance from pole stay wires; navigate to a predetermined destination at altitude below 500 ft AGL; comply with airspace requirements and procedures; demonstrate correct navigation techniques and procedures at low level; correctly perform low level circuit and landing; correctly perform after landing and shutdown checks. **LL-H.5 – Execute autorotative forced landing (simulated) from below 500 ft AGL (single‑engine helicopter only)** identify potential forced-landing areas prior to and during low-level operations; recognise engine failure or any other emergency requiring a forced landing and conduct recall actions; maintain control of the aircraft – select the most appropriate landing area within gliding distance while avoiding any powerlines or obstructions; manoeuvre the aircraft to a landing area that achieves the safest outcome; explain plan of action and the landing techniques that would ensure the safest outcome when committed to a forced landing on unfavourable terrain or water. **LL-H.6 – Execute engine failure (simulated) from below 500 ft AGL (multi-engine helicopter only)** identify potential escape routes prior to and during low-level operations; recognise engine failure or any other emergency and conduct recall actions; maintain control of the aircraft – initiate climb to safe altitude; manoeuvre the aircraft via escape route to a safe altitude; complete check system items; explain plan of action. **LL-H.7 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the aeroplane at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR; approved helicopter with dual controls, electronic intercom and dual control brakes if fitted; aerodromes or HLS; hazards may include variable terrain and weather, surface conditions, other aircraft, lose objects, personnel, animals, birds propeller wash, rotor wash, jet blast and negative ‘g’ in teetering rotor systems; limitations may be imposed by local noise abatement procedures and curfews.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.5, Low-level rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; maximum rate and minimum rate turn criteria; the effect of wind velocity in low-level operations; the effect of aircraft inertia at low level; effects of illusions; obstruction avoidance techniques; critical operational conditions, including retreating blade stall, vortex ring, over pitching loss of anti-torque effectiveness and negative ‘g’ effects; meteorological factors affecting helicopter performance at low level; terrain following techniques; safety hazards and risks of low-level operations and methods of control.

LL-PL Powered-lift aircraft low-level operations – *Reserved*

LL-G Gyroplane low-level operations

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to manoeuvre a gyroplane safely and effectively at low level, in accordance with the following provisions.

Elements and performance criteria **LL-G.1 – Plan low-level operations** identifies, evaluates and manages risks at low level; complete consultation with all stake holders involved in the low-level operation to confirm task requirements; ensures aircraft type and performance is appropriate for the task; assesses and allows for the effects of fatigue and physical health on pilot performance; analyses and applies actual and forecast weather conditions to low-level operations; identifies area of operations using chart and geographical features; assesses geographical characteristics of the area of flying operations to ensure safe completion of the task; identifies and avoid all significant obstructions; identifies and avoids buildings, personnel, vehicles, animals, vegetation and nuisance areas **LL-G.2 – Flight component** correctly performs pre-flight inspection and determine aircraft serviceability for intended flight; initialises and checks data validity of area navigation system (if fitted); correctly operates aircraft; correctly performs take-off. **LL-G.3 – Aircraft handling** at an altitude above 1,500 ft AGL: conducts pre-manoeuvre checks; performs an effective lookout; demonstrates level flight, climbing and descending turns up to 60° angle of bank; visual references utilised; speed monitored; bank attitude maintained; pitch attitude adjusted for bank angle; desired altitude maintained; lookout performed; rollout and level off anticipated; demonstrates approach and recovery to stall in level flight; clearing turns; configures aircraft; recognises approach to stall conditions; maintains references by visual cues; recovers by AOA reduction (consistent with available height) and power application; demonstrates approach and recovery to stall in turning flight; clearing turns; configures aircraft; recognises approach to stall conditions; maintains references by visual cues; recovers by AOA reduction (consistent with available height) and power application; applies correct techniques for upset recovery in various configurations; clearing turns; configures aircraft; recognises approach to stall conditions; maintains references by visual cues; identifies the approach to stall; recovers by AOA reduction (consistent with available height);
