demonstrates maximum rate turning; knows maximum performance turning criteria; area cleared; maximum power applied; maximum bank applied for turning performance commensurate with speed; maximum permitted ‘g’ applied commensurate with speed; achieves turning at maximum AOA; aircraft does not stall or exceed permitted ‘g’ limits; performs lookout; anticipates rollout; releases ‘g’ force during roll out of turn; demonstrates minimum radius turning; knows minimum radius turning criteria; area cleared; maximum power applied; height as low as practical (1,500 ft AGL); maximum AOA maintained; aircraft does not stall; performs lookout; anticipates rollout; releases ‘g’ forces while rolling out of the turn; demonstrates methods of losing height in a turn and straight flight; manages the energy state of the aircraft; identifies high kinetic energy situations; identifies low kinetic energy situations; identifies high potential energy situations; identifies low potential energy situations. **LL-G.4 – Low level handling** at an altitude of 200 ft AGL but not below 50 ft AGL: manage the aircraft energy state; perform straight flight: adjust height according to terrain to maintain assigned height above ground level; recognise and manage the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; compensate for drift; perform turning at various bank angles up to 60° angle of bank at normal cruise speed; adjust power as required; recognise and manage the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; compensate for the effect of gradient wind; anticipate rollout; demonstrate use of escape routes and rising ground; demonstrate flight at various speed and configurations not below minimum safe speed + 15 KIAS; operate adjacent to powerlines and wires; demonstrate awareness of wind effect in the vicinity of obstructions, mountainous terrain and illusions; recognise and control the illusion of slipping and skidding during turns in windy conditions; recognise the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; maintain a constant altitude over featureless terrain or water; conduct procedure turns from a fixed ground reference point; demonstrate knowledge of the effect of false horizons; recognise and manage impact of sun glare on increased risk of collision with obstacles; identify the requirement to operate in the vicinity of powerlines and wires and assesses risk; identify and avoid powerlines (wires) by a minimum of 15 ft (-0 ft) when crossed overhead by an aircraft; identify and avoid all powerlines and wires; identify poles, cross trees, wires and insulators to assist powerline and wire location; identify and avoid pole stay wires; navigate to a predetermined destination at altitude below 500 ft AGL; maintain a constant altitude over featureless terrain or water; conduct procedure turns from a fixed ground reference point; comply with airspace requirements and procedures; demonstrate correct navigation techniques and procedures at low level; correctly perform low-level circuit and landing; correctly perform after landing and shutdown checks. **LL-G.5 – Execute autorotative forced landing (simulated) from below 500 ft AGL (single‑engine gyrocopter only)** identify potential forced-landing areas prior to and during low-level operations; recognise engine failure or any other emergency requiring a forced landing and conduct recall actions; maintain control of the aircraft – select the most appropriate landing area within gliding distance while avoiding any powerlines or obstructions; manoeuvre the aircraft to a landing area that achieves the safest outcome; explain plan of action and the landing techniques that would ensure the safest outcome when committed to a forced landing on unfavourable terrain or water. **LL-G.6 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the aeroplane at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR; approved gyroplane dual controls, electronic intercom and dual control brakes if fitted; aerodromes or landing areas; hazards may include variable terrain and weather, surface conditions, other aircraft, lose objects, personnel, animals, birds propeller wash, rotor wash, jet blast and negative ‘g’ in teetering rotor systems; limitations may be imposed by local noise abatement procedures and curfews.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.5, Low-level rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; maximum rate and minimum rate turn criteria; the effect of wind velocity in low-level operations; the effect of aircraft inertia at low level; effects of illusions; obstruction avoidance techniques; critical operational conditions, including retreating blade stall, blade flap, and negative ‘g’ effects; meteorological factors affecting performance at low level; terrain following techniques; safety hazards and risks of low-level operations and methods of control.

LL-M Aerial mustering operations

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct aerial mustering operations.

Elements and performance criteria **LL-M.1 – Plan a stock mustering operation**

Formulate a stock mustering operation plan, including:

determination of location and boundaries of the area of operation, terrain features;

suitability and serviceability of aircraft, starting point, positioning of support personnel, final destination of stock, location and suitability of landing areas;

present and forecast weather;

methods of communication and signals;

hazards and obstructions;

emergency procedures to ensure the safe and effective operation.

**LL-M.2 – Manoeuvre aircraft to the limits of the flight-manoeuvring envelope** manoeuvre aircraft in all planes below 500 ft AGL, up to and not beyond the limits of the flight-manoeuvring envelope, without exceeding the operating limitations of the aircraft; in addition to the performance criterion in paragraph (a), for helicopters, perform reversal turns, decelerations, steep turns, climb and descent manoeuvres, low and high speed manoeuvres within the following standards: ensure power available exceeds power required; conduct hovering only when OGE power is available for the gross weight, density altitude and relative wind conditions; avoid conditions conducive to loss of tail rotor effectiveness; avoid negative ‘g’ and reduced disc loading flight manoeuvres in teetering main rotor head systems; avoid vortex ring conditions during quick stop/deceleration manoeuvres and recovery from low airspeed descending manoeuvres; remain below VMAX and VNE limits; comply with weight/velocity avoid combinations; in addition to the performance criterion in paragraph (a), for gyroplanes, perform reversal turns, decelerations, steep turns, climb and descent manoeuvres, low and high speed manoeuvres within the following standards: manoeuvre the gyroplane at speeds above the speed that ensures the gyroplane is not ‘behind the power curve’ (power available is greater than power required); avoid negative ‘g’ manoeuvres; VMAX and VNE limits are not exceeded; balances gyroplane.

**LL-M.3 – General manoeuvring** achieves desired ground tracks; maintains visual contact with the ground; manages the effect of wind and turbulence.

**LL-M.4 – Conduct a stock mustering operation using an aircraft** coordinates and conducts the assembly and movement of stock to predetermined destination in the time available, safely and effectively, using an aircraft; establishes and maintains an effective communication system with stock mustering people on the ground.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR; for the aerial mustering – aeroplane endorsement, the aircraft must be an aeroplane; for the aerial mustering – helicopter endorsement, the aircraft must be an helicopter; for the aerial mustering – gyroplane endorsement, the aircraft must be an gyroplane; obstructions and vertical terrain; up to and including light turbulence; simulated emergency or abnormal situations; simulated hazardous weather; stock.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.5, Low-level rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; maximum rate and minimum rate turn criteria; the effect of wind velocity in low-level operations; the effect of aircraft inertia at low level; effects of illusions; obstruction avoidance techniques; critical operational conditions, including, aerodynamic stall, retreating blade stall, blade flap, and negative ‘g’ effects; meteorological factors affecting performance at low level; terrain following techniques; safety hazards and risks of low-level operations and methods of control.

LL-SO Sling operations

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct sling operations.

Elements and performance criteria **LL-SO.1 – Prepare and rig a sling load** tasking requirements are identified; external load is secured, stabilised and rigged in accordance with workplace procedures and AFM or POH. **LL-SO.2 – Plan external load operations** external load procedure, equipment and personnel required for task are determined; helicopter performance data is interpreted and calculated to ensure suitability of aircraft for external load operations; outbound and return flight routes are planned; secure and stable load preparations are arranged; load lifting equipment strength and suitability are assessed. **LL-SO.3 – Conduct pre-flight briefings for external load operations** requirements of the load task are explained and confirmed; personnel responsible for inspecting the load lifting equipment for serviceability and security are identified; communication and hook-up procedure is explained; hook-up person and hook-up procedure is specified; departure, transit, approach, termination and load release procedures are explained; emergency procedures are explained and confirmed; pilot vertical reference (long line) procedure is explained if applicable; crew and ground loadmaster are briefed on all aspects of the load lifting task; seating is adjusted to ensure full exercise of the flight controls and the ability to scan the instrument panel; helicopter performance data is interpreted and calculated to ensure suitability of aircraft for operations; the removal of doors and the security of internal equipment is arranged as required. **LL-SO.4 – Operate the aircraft during external load operations** functional and safety checks on role equipment are performed, and defects are reported; fuel and cargo load combinations to achieve task are calculated; adequacy of power margin and directional control are determined; stable hover over the load during hook-up/delivery procedures is maintained; external load is lifted and transported to a separate location and placed at a specified position; load is monitored and appropriate actions are taken to ensure load security and stability during flight; excessive load swing during transit is avoided. **LL-SO.5 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations during external load operations** helicopter control is maintained; abnormal or emergency situations are identified and managed in accordance with workplace procedures and AFM or POH; load is jettisoned when appropriate. **LL-SO.6 – Conduct post-flight activities for external load operations** operating procedures and outcomes of the flight are reviewed and analysed; effectiveness, efficiency and performance of equipment is analysed and reported.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; tasks that may be undertaken in variable weather in day VFR and NVFR conditions; performance must be demonstrated in: an aircraft capable of hovering; variable air traffic conditions; variable flight situations; abnormal situations; performance must be demonstrated on aircraft with: fully functioning dual controls; an electronic intercom system; dual control brakes; wheeled or skidded undercarriages; NVFR environment may include: unaided; aided utilising night vision devices; crew may include: single pilot; multi-crew; load lifting may be carried out: with crewman; without crewman.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.5, Low-level rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; relevant sections of Civil Aviation Safety Regulations and Civil Aviation Orders; engine performance checks for the helicopter type to be flown; aircraft performance calculations (for all phases of flight); internal and external load limitations for the aircraft type to be flown; aerial delivery equipment operation, safe working loads and limitations; cargo hook limitations, problems and hazards; load rigging and preparation for flight; principles of aerodynamics; control effectiveness in all phases of flight; hazards that exist and problems that can occur when operating an aircraft during external load operations; procedures to address problems associated with a helicopter during external load operations; aircraft dimensions; vertical reference (long line) operation procedures if applicable; external load lifting equipment inspection procedures; communication procedure and terminology applicable to external load operations.

LL-WR Winch and rappelling operations

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct winch and rappelling operations.

Elements and performance criteria **LL-WR.1 – Plan roping operations** tasking requirements are identified; crew roping personnel and equipment required to ensure safe achievement of task are determined; aircraft performance is interpreted and calculated to ensure suitability of aircraft for roping operations; transit, roping operation communications and recovery is planned in accordance with workplace procedures; roping personnel qualifications are confirmed; roping operations abnormal and emergency situation actions are planned. **LL-WR.2 – Conduct pre-flight briefings for roping operations** requirements of the roping operation are explained and confirmed; location, terrain features (sea state as applicable) and forecast weather conditions are obtained and confirmed; timings, route(s), airspeeds and altitudes are confirmed; pilot, crew and roping personnel responsibilities and communication procedures are explained; roping operation emergency procedures are explained. **LL-WR.3 – Operate the helicopter during roping operations** site inspection, approach and hover heading are determined in accordance with operational requirements; descent and approach is controlled to terminate over the roping site; adequacy of hover power margin and control limits to perform roping operations is checked and maintained; control is applied to the aircraft to maintain position over roping site; obstacle clearances are maintained during roping operations; crew member is directed/cleared to deploy ropes; roping team is directed when clear to perform roping operation in accordance with workplace procedures; ropes are recovered/detached and site vacated in accordance with workplace procedures. **LL-WR.4 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations during roping operations** aircraft control is maintained; abnormal or emergency situations are identified and managed in accordance with workplace procedure and AFMAFM or POH. **LL-WR.5 – Conduct post-flight briefings for roping operations** operating procedures and outcomes of the flight are reviewed and analysed; effectiveness, efficiency and performance of equipment is analysed and reported.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; tasks may be undertaken in variable weather conditions in accordance with day VFR and NVFR; performance may be demonstrated in: an aircraft capable of hovering; variable air traffic conditions; variable flight situations; abnormal situations; performance must be demonstrated on a helicopter or tilt rotor aircraft with: fully functioning dual controls; an electronic intercom system; dual control brakes; wheeled or skidded undercarriages; night aided vision devices; NVFR environment may include: unaided; aided utilising night vision devices; operational environments may include: unprepared landing sites; confined areas; unknown landing sites; pinnacles; embarked/sea platforms; marine environments; crew may include: single pilot; multi-crew; limitations may be imposed by local noise abatement requirements and curfews; roping may include: rappelling; fast rope; checklists may include: AFM or POH approach and landing; hover; pre-roping; class of airspace are: those designated by CASA; restricted and danger areas; military control zones; Air Defence identification zones; operational hazards during low-level operations may include: structures; other aircraft; loose objects; birds; engine salt ingestion; trees; dust; low visibility; turbulence; wind strength; sea state; guidance during low-level operations may be provided by: air traffic control instructions; light signals; aerodrome markings; procedures for maintaining compliance with airspace requirements are: geographical limits of the flight area are demonstrated on a chart; prominent geographical features are identified using a chart; the limits of the flight area are identified on the ground; the position of controlled airspace is determined using a chart and geographical features; restricted areas are identified using a chart and geographical features; departure from the circuit (roping) area and transition to the flight area is completed without incident; departure from the flight area and transition to the circuit (roping) area is completed without incident; dependent on the type of organisation concerned and the local terminology used, workplace procedures may include: company procedures; enterprise procedures; organisational procedures; established procedures; standard operating procedures; information/documents may include: relevant sections of CASR 1998 and CAOs, including day VFR; in Defence context, relevant Defence Orders and Instructions; AFM or POH; this MOS; AIP; ERSA; charts; operations manuals; approved checklists; workplace procedures and instructions and job specification; induction and training materials; conditions of service, legislation and industrial agreements, including workplace agreements and awards; applicable regulations and legislation may include: relevant CASR 1998 and CAOs; in Defence context, relevant Defence Orders and Instructions; relevant state/territory OH&S legislation; relevant state/territory environmental protection legislation; relevant Australian Standards; performance includes tolerances specified in either of: relevant licence and aircraft rating requirements of as this MOS: relevant Defence documentation such as: Defence Orders and Instructions; approved curricula and training documentation.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: the topics mentioned in Section 2.5, Low-level rating in Schedule 3 of this MOS; relevant sections of CASR 1998 and CAOs; relevant OH&S and environmental procedures and regulations; in Defence context, relevant Defence Orders and Instructions; communication procedure and terminology applicable to roping operations; engine performance checks for the helicopter type to be flown; aircraft performance calculations (for all phases of flight); internal and external load limitations for the helicopter type to be flown, including weight and balance consideration; functions and effects of all aircraft controls and instruments; principles of aerodynamics: control effectiveness in all phases of flight; hazards, limitations and problems that can occur when operating an aircraft during roping operations; rope and attaching point limitations; helicopter dimensions.

AERIAL APPLICATION RATING

AA1 Aeroplane aerial application operation

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct aerial application operations other than firefighting operations in aeroplanes.

Elements and performance criteria **AA1.1 – Pre-flight actions** conduct self-assessment fit for flight and planned operation; determine suitability of aircraft for type of operation; conduct a thorough pre-flight of aircraft and role equipment to determine serviceability for planned operations; check and correctly complete required maintenance documentation as applicable; confirm minimum equipment and minimum crew and instrumentation requirements for planned operations are met; check safe operation of role equipment, including the serviceability of the jettison (dump) door; check and adjust role equipment calibration; planning and risk management; determine the requirement to operate at low level; identifies hazards, analyses the risks and implement a decision to safely conduct low-level operations – ensures aeroplane type and performance is appropriate for the task; assesses and allows for the effects of fatigue and physical health on pilot performance; analyses and applies actual and forecast weather conditions to low-level operations; develop an Application Management Plan; correctly interpret treatment area map; understands that all aircraft limitations, except those exempted by CASA (maximum take-off weight), are applicable to the operation; adequately identify potential hazards and operational requirements, assess risks and apply appropriate risk controls, including powerlines, houses, susceptible crops and environmentally sensitive areas; demonstrate an ability to make a command decision on the safety or otherwise of the proposed application, including refusing to undertake an application where the risks are considered to be too high; make appropriate selection of application pattern and direction of treatment taking into consideration safety, efficiency, hazards and terrain; carefully plans fuel requirements; confirms acceptable aircraft performance for conditions; confirms location of ground support personnel when available; confirms normal and abnormal ops communications and signals; confirms appropriate logistical considerations, including local airstrip condition, fuel, products, ground support and access to strip, SARWATCH, water, and personal supplies, including adequate water and food. **AA1.2 – Fly to, assess, land and take-off from an operational airstrip** performs low-level navigation to an operational airstrip at an appropriate height; performs appropriate assessment of an operational airstrip, including strip length, conditions, direction, identification of hazards, meteorological conditions; selects the most suitable loading area; correctly performs pre-landing and pre-take-off checks; selects a ‘no go, go around, commitment’ point for landings; selects a touchdown point for landings; identifies and manages issues relating to aircraft weight, performance, strip length, slope, surface, direction, load, surrounds, hazards and meteorological conditions; demonstrates appropriate short-field landing and take-off techniques, including having her or his hand on the dump door handle for take-offs and being prepared to dump if required; identifies an appropriate dumping point for each take-off, including adequate safety buffers; demonstrates safe operations from a 1-way airstrip. **AA1.3 – Fly between operational airstrip and application area** performs low-level navigation from an operational airstrip to an application area; selects the most appropriate route and height between the operational strip and application area with considerations to terrain, stock, populated areas, housing and hazards. **AA1.4 – Conduct operations at a certified or registered aerodrome**

Performs operations in accordance with the requirements published regulations.

**AA1.5 – Conduct an aerial survey of a treatment area** develops an appropriate and safe plan for conduct of an aerial survey; accurately identifies the treatment area boundaries; confirms the map; identifies susceptible crops and environmentally sensitive areas; identifies hazards on the map; identifies potential emergency landing area(s); checks and identifies any hazards not on the map, including sun glare and shadows from hills; accurately assesses wind speed and direction; identifies clean-up runs required; confirms or appropriately amends the Application Management Plan, including pattern type and direction of treatment and possible suspension of application if conditions are not appropriate.

**AA1.6 – Fly aircraft at low level**

Identifies and avoids buildings, personnel, vehicles, animals, vegetation and nuisance areas.

**AA1.7 – Perform steep turns and procedure turns at or below 500 ft AGL** performs airspace cleared procedure; conducts a balanced steep turn level (± 100 ft) climbing and descending turn at a nominated speed; conducts procedure turns with varying flap and power settings.

**AA1.8 – Manoeuvre and navigate at low level** manoeuvres aeroplane at a height below 500 ft AGL; navigates an aeroplane to a predetermined destination at altitudes at or below 500 ft AGL; awareness of wind effect in the vicinity obstructions, mountainous terrain and illusions; identifies wind velocity; recognises and controls the illusions of slipping and skidding during turns in windy conditions; recognises and manages impact of sun glare on increased risk of collision with obstacles; operate adjacent to powerlines and wires; identifies the requirement to operate in the vicinity of powerlines and wires and assesses risk; identifies poles, cross trees, wires and insulators to assist powerline and wire location; recognises and manages the effect of rising and descending terrain on aircraft performance; demonstrate safe operation from non-certified or registered landing areas; accurately re-enters treatment area with aircraft aligned for treatment run; accurately identifies and monitors wind speed and direction; recognises and manages the adverse effects of wind caused by terrain and obstructions; recognises and manages false horizon illusions; maintains a constant altitude over featureless terrain or water; establishes and maintains an appropriate height and speed over treatment area.

**AA1.9 – Recognise and avoid the stall and recover from a simulated low altitude stall** recognises the approach to the stall during any phase of flight and resumes normal balanced flight before stall entry; recovers from a developed stall at a simulated altitude of 500 ft AGL by a simulated altitude of 300 ft AGL. Minimum actual attitude is to be not below 3,000 ft.

**AA1.10 – Execute forced landing from below 500 ft AGL** identifies potential forced-landing areas prior to and during low-level operations; recognises engine failure or any other emergency requiring a forced landing and conducts recall actions; maintains control of the aircraft – selects the most appropriate landing area within gliding distance while avoiding any powerlines or obstructions; manoeuvres the aircraft to a landing area that achieves the safest outcome; explains plan of action and the landing techniques that would ensure the safest outcome when committed to a forced landing on unfavourable terrain or water.

**AA1.11 – Conduct operations over and under powerlines** identifies powerlines both in and outside the treatment area during an aerial survey; demonstrates an ability to interpret powerline infrastructure cues so as to aid wire run identification; demonstrates safe technique for accurately assessing wire height, including safe flying parallel to wires; identifies and manages other hazards relevant to operations near powerlines, such as pole stays, crop height, fences or machinery that may pose a risk; demonstrates safe command decisions whether to fly over or under a wire; conducts safe treatment over wires, including adequate safety buffers for pull-up and let‑down and accurate cut-off and on of application equipment; conducts safe treatment under wires, including safe clearance; terminates approaches towards powerlines when passage beneath is unachievable; can explain the relevant human factors that may affect operations near powerlines, particularly distraction, short-term memory limitations and in attentional blindness.

**AA1.12 – Apply substances** safely applies substances in accordance with application management plan; establishes and maintains correct application height relevant to terrain, application type and meteorological conditions; controls airspeed and flight profile appropriately on entry/re-entry to treatment area; engages and shuts off application equipment at appropriate points; manoeuvers around and over hazards in the treatment area with adequate safety buffers; regularly uses aircraft smoker to identify and monitor wind direction; monitors application flow rate, pressure and product remaining; conducts clean-up runs, including extra safety check for hazards; demonstrates safe command decisions to continue with, amend or suspend operations due to changing conditions.

**AA1.13 – Operate aircraft safely and effectively using GNSS swath guidance equipment** demonstrates basic familiarity with at least 1 GNSS system; demonstrates sound judgement in selecting the correct pattern relevant to the treatment area and terrain; selects correct swath relevant to the aircraft, aircraft configuration and the substance to be applied; accurately places an AB line and C point if required; manoeuvres the aircraft accurately on the correct swath line with reference to the light bar and natural features; operate aircraft at maximum permissible weights for aerial application operations; determines take-off weight within legal requirements and relevant to strip length and conditions; operates safely and effectively at maximum weights during: taxi; take off and climb; approach and landing (including safe command decisions on dumping and strip selection); application; turns; obstacle avoidance.

**AA1.14 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the aircraft at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows.

**AA1.15 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations during low-level operations** identifies potential forced-landing areas prior to and during aerial application operations; identifies abnormal or emergency situation; conducts appropriate abnormal or emergency procedures during application operations; maintains control of the aircraft, jettisons load if required, and avoids any powerlines or hazards; successfully conducts a practice forced landing from 500 ft.

**AA1.16 – Jettison load** jettisons a full liquid load during take-off prior to lift off, and maintains control of the aircraft; jettison a full liquid load immediately after take-off and maintains control of the aircraft; jettisons a full liquid load during flight and controls pitch changes to ensure maintenance of altitude (+100/-0 ft) by adjustments of elevator and power.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR in variable weather conditions; approved aircraft; approved low-flying areas; operational airstrips; man-made or natural obstacles; undulating, hilly or mountainous terrain; emergency and abnormal situations; hazardous weather conditions; mental and physical fatigue; heat stress and dehydration; maintaining situational awareness; in-flight distractions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: CASA exemptions with regards to maximum take-off weight and applicability of other aircraft limitations; applicable regulations that relate to the conduct of a safe operation; low level meteorology; relevant aerodynamics and aircraft performance; aircraft flight manual, performance, engine and systems; human factors; safety hazards and risks of flight at low level; role equipment; factors to be considered when determining the payload weight for each application; aircraft configuration for the aircraft being flown, when jettisoning a full load; characteristics of the aircraft being flown when jettisoning a full load; flight control and throttle actions required to maintain control of the aircraft being flown when jettisoning a full load.

AA2 Helicopter aerial application operation

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct aerial application operations other than firefighting operations in helicopters.

Elements and performance criteria **AA2.1 – Pre-flight actions** conduct self-assessment fit for flight and planned operation; determine suitability of helicopter for type of operation; conduct a thorough pre-flight of helicopter and role equipment to determine serviceability for planned operations; check and correctly complete required maintenance documentation as applicable; confirm minimum equipment and minimum crew and instrumentation requirements for planned operations are met; check safe operation of role equipment, including the serviceability of the jettison (dump) door if applicable or the sling jettison; check and adjust role equipment calibration. **AA2.2 – Planning and risk management** determine the requirement to operate at low level, analyses the risk and implement a decision to safely conduct low-level operations; develop an Application Management Plan; correctly interpret treatment area map; adequately identify potential hazards and operational requirements, assess risks and apply appropriate risk controls, including powerlines, houses, susceptible crops and environmentally sensitive areas; demonstrate an ability to make a command decision on the safety or otherwise of the proposed application, including refusing to undertake an application where the risks are considered to be too high; determine the suitability of the current and forecast weather; make appropriate selection of application pattern and direction of treatment taking into consideration safety, efficiency, hazards and terrain; carefully plans fuel requirements; confirms acceptable helicopter performance for conditions; confirms location of ground support personnel when available; confirms normal and abnormal ops communications and signals; confirms appropriate logistical considerations, including local HLS condition, fuel, products, ground support and access to HLS, SARWACH, water, and personal supplies, including adequate water and food. **AA2.3 – Fly to, assess, land and take-off from an operational HLS** performs low-level navigation to an operational HLS at an appropriate height; performs appropriate assessment of an operational HLS, including dimensions, conditions, direction, identification of hazards, meteorological conditions; identifies and manages issues relating to helicopter weight, performance, dimensions, load and meteorological conditions; consistently performs pre-landing and pre-take-off checks; demonstrates appropriate landing and take-off techniques; identifies an appropriate dumping point for each take-off, including adequate safety buffers; demonstrates safe operations from a marginal HLS. **AA2.4 – Fly between operational HLS and application area** performs low-level navigation from an operational HLS to an application area; selects the most appropriate route and height between the operational HLS and application area with considerations to terrain, stock, populated areas, housing and hazards; conduct operations at a certified or registered aerodrome; performs operations in accordance with the requirements of published regulations. **AA2.5 – Conduct an aerial survey of a treatment area** develops an appropriate and safe plan for conduct of an aerial survey; accurately identifies the treatment area boundaries; confirms the map; identifies susceptible crops and environmentally sensitive areas; identifies hazards on the map; identifies potential emergency landing area(s); checks and identifies any hazards not on the map, including sun glare and shadows from hills; accurately assesses wind speed and direction; identifies clean-up runs required; confirms or appropriately amends the Application Management Plan, including pattern type and direction of treatment and possible suspension of application if conditions are not appropriate. **AA2.6 – Manipulate helicopter at low level** manoeuvres helicopter at all speeds below 500 ft AGL, up to and not beyond the limits of the flight-manoeuvring envelope, without exceeding the operating limitations of the helicopter; conducts coordinated, smooth procedure (P) turns with varying power settings; accurately re-enters treatment area with helicopter aligned for treatment run; accurately identifies and monitors wind speed and direction; recognises and manages the adverse effects of wind caused by terrain and obstructions; recognises and controls the illusions caused by turning in windy conditions; manages the effects of gradient wind; recognises and manages the effect of rising and descending terrain on helicopter performance; recognises and manages false horizon illusions; maintains a constant altitude over featureless terrain or water; establishes and maintains an appropriate height and speed over treatment area. **AA2.7 – Conduct operations over and under powerlines** identifies powerlines both in and outside the treatment area during an aerial survey; demonstrates an ability to interpret powerline infrastructure cues so as to aid wire run identification; demonstrates safe technique for accurately assessing wire height, including safe flying parallel to wires; identifies and manages other hazards relevant to operations near powerlines, such as pole stays, crop height, fences or machinery that may pose a risk; demonstrates safe command decisions whether to fly over or under a wire; conducts safe treatment over wires, including adequate safety buffers for pull-up and let‑down and accurate cut-off and on of application equipment; conducts safe treatment under wires, including safe clearance; terminates approaches towards powerlines when passage beneath is unachievable; can explain the relevant human factors that may affect operations near powerlines, particularly distraction, short-term memory limitations and inattentional (perceptual) blindness. **AA2.8 – Apply substances** safely applies substances in accordance with application management plan; establishes and maintains correct application height relevant to terrain, application type and meteorological conditions; controls airspeed and flight profile appropriately on entry and re-entry to treatment area; engages and shuts off application equipment at appropriate points; manoeuvers around and over hazards in the treatment area with adequate safety buffers; regularly uses aircraft smoker to identify and monitor wind direction; monitors application flow rate, pressure and product remaining; conducts clean-up runs, including extra safety check for hazards; demonstrates safe command decisions to continue with, amend or suspend operations due to changing conditions. **AA2.9 – Operate helicopter safely and effectively using GNSS swath guidance equipment** demonstrates basic familiarity with at least 1 GNSS system; demonstrates sound judgement in selecting the correct pattern relevant to the treatment area and terrain; selects correct swath relevant to the helicopter, helicopter configuration and the substance to be applied; accurately places an AB line and C point if required; manoeuvres the helicopter accurately on the correct swath line with reference to the light bar and natural features; operate helicopter at maximum permissible weights for aerial application operations; determines take-off weight within legal requirements and relevant to HLS dimensions and conditions; operates safely and effectively at maximum weights during: hover and taxi; take off and climb; approach and landing (including command decision on dumping and HLS selection); application; turns; obstacle avoidance. **AA2.10 – Manage known helicopter risks during application operations** demonstrate sound decision making in assessing likely hover performance considering load, density altitude, ground surface and relative wind; demonstrates awareness of, and sound behaviours in, managing rotor disc behaviour under reduced or negative ‘g’; demonstrates awareness of, and sound behaviour in, avoiding dynamic rollover; demonstrates awareness of, and sound behaviour in, avoiding loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE). **AA2.11 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the helicopter at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows; manage abnormal and emergency situations during low-level operations; identifies potential forced-landing areas prior to and during aerial application operations; identifies abnormal or emergency situation; conducts appropriate abnormal or emergency procedures during application operations; maintains control of helicopter, including adequate coordination of collective, jettisons load if required, and avoids any powerlines or hazards; successfully conducts a practice forced landing from 500 ft. **AA2.12 – Jettison load** jettisons a full liquid load during take-off and maintains control of the helicopter; jettisons a full liquid load during flight and controls pitch changes.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR in variable weather conditions; approved helicopter; approved low-flying areas; operational HLSs; man-made or natural obstacles; undulating, hilly or mountainous terrain; emergency and abnormal situations; hazardous weather conditions; mental and physical fatigue; heat stress and dehydration; maintaining situational awareness; in-flight distractions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: applicable regulations that relate to the conduct of a safe operation; low level meteorology; relevant aerodynamics and helicopter performance; helicopter flight manual, performance, engine and systems; relevant human factors; safety hazards and risks of flight at low level; role equipment; factors to be considered when determining the payload weight for each application; helicopter configuration for the helicopter being flown, when jettisoning a full load; flight characteristics of the helicopter being flown when jettisoning a full load; flight control and throttle actions required to maintain control of the helicopter being flown when jettisoning a full load.

AA3 Gyroplane aerial application operation

1 Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct aerial application operations other than firefighting operations in gyroplanes.

2 Elements and performance criteria

2.1 AA3.1 – Pre-flight actions

(a) self-assess personal fitness for flight and planned operation;

(b) determine suitability of gyroplane for type of operation;

(c) conduct pre-flight of gyroplane and role equipment to determine serviceability for planned operations;

(d) check and complete required maintenance documentation as applicable;

(e) confirm minimum equipment and minimum crew and instrumentation requirements for planned operations are met;

(f) check operation of role equipment, including the serviceability of the jettison (dump) door;

(g) check and adjust role equipment calibration;

(h) planning and risk management;

(i) determine the requirement to operate at low level;

(j) identify hazards, analyse the risks and implement a decision to safely conduct low‑level operations – ensure gyroplane type and performance is appropriate for the task;

(k) assess and allow for the effects of fatigue and physical health on pilot performance;

(l) analyse and apply actual and forecast weather conditions to low-level operations;

(m) develop an aerial application management plan;

(n) interpret treatment area map;

(o) understand that aircraft limitations apply to the operation except those exempted by CASA (maximum take-off weight);

(p) identify potential hazards and operational requirements, assess risks and apply risk controls, including powerlines, houses, susceptible crops and environmentally‑sensitive areas;

(q) demonstrate an ability to make a command decision on the safety or otherwise of the proposed application, including refusing to undertake an application where the risks are considered to be too high;

(r) make appropriate selection of application pattern and direction of treatment taking into consideration safety, efficiency, hazards and terrain;

(s) plan fuel requirements;

(t) confirm acceptable aircraft performance for conditions;

(u) confirm location of ground support personnel;

(v) confirm normal and abnormal ops communications and signals;

(w) confirm logistical considerations are in place, including local airstrip condition, fuel, products, ground support and access to strip, SARWATCH, water, and personal supplies, including adequate water and food.

2.2 AA3.2 – Fly to, assess, land and take off from an operational airstrip

(a) perform low-level navigation to an operational airstrip at an appropriate height;

(b) perform assessment of an operational airstrip, including strip length, conditions, direction, identification of hazards, meteorological conditions;

(c) select the most suitable loading area;

(d) perform pre-landing and pre-take-off checks;

(e) select a ‘no go, go around, commitment’ point for landings;

(f) select a touchdown point for landings;

(g) identify and manage issues relating to aircraft weight, performance, strip length, slope, surface, direction, load, surrounds, hazards and meteorological conditions;

(h) demonstrate appropriate short-field landing and take-off techniques and being prepared to dump if required;

(i) identify an appropriate dumping point for each take-off, including adequate safety buffers;

(j) demonstrate operations from a 1-way airstrip.

2.3 AA3.3 – Fly between operational airstrip and application area

(a) perform low-level navigation from an operational airstrip to an application area;

(b) select the most appropriate route and height between the operational strip and application area considering terrain, stock, populated areas, housing and hazards.

2.4 AA3.4 – Conduct operations at a certified aerodrome

Perform operations in accordance with the published procedures and requirements.

2.5 AA3.5 – Conduct an aerial survey of a treatment area

(a) develop an appropriate plan for conduct of an aerial survey;

(b) identify the treatment area boundaries;

(c) confirm map accuracy;

(d) identify susceptible crops and environmentally-sensitive areas;

(e) identify hazards on the map;

(f) identify potential emergency landing area(s);

(g) check and identify any hazards not on the map, including sun glare and shadows from hills;

(h) assess wind speed and direction;

(i) identify clean-up runs required;

(j) confirm or amend the aerial application management plan, including pattern type and direction of treatment and possible suspension of application if conditions are not acceptable.

2.6 AA3.6 – Fly gyroplane at low level

Identify and avoid buildings, personnel, vehicles, animals, vegetation and nuisance areas.

2.7 AA3.7 – Perform steep turns and procedure turns at or below 500 ft AGL

(a) conduct balanced steep-level (±100 ft) climbing and descending turns at a nominated speed;

(b) conduct procedure turns with varying power settings.

2.8 AA3.8 – Manoeuvre and navigate at low level

(a) manoeuvre gyroplane at a height below 500 ft AGL;

(b) navigate gyroplane to a predetermined destination at altitudes at or below 500 ft AGL;

(c) demonstrate awareness of wind effect in the vicinity of obstructions, mountainous terrain and illusions;

(d) identify wind velocity;

(e) recognise and manage illusions of slipping and skidding during turns in windy conditions;

(f) recognise and manage impact of sun glare on increased risk of collision with obstacles;

(g) operate adjacent to powerlines and wires;

(h) identify requirement to operate in the vicinity of powerlines and wires and manage risk;

(i) identify poles, cross trees, wires and insulators to assist powerline and wire location;

(j) recognise and manage effect of rising and descending terrain on gyroplane performance;

(k) demonstrate operation from non-certified or registered landing areas;

(l) re-enter treatment area with gyroplane aligned for treatment run;

(m) identify and monitor wind speed and direction;

(n) recognise and manage adverse effects of wind caused by terrain and obstructions;

(o) recognise and manage false horizon illusions;

(p) maintain a constant altitude over featureless terrain or water;

(q) establish and maintain appropriate height and speed over treatment area.

2.9 AA3.9 – Manage flight at low speed and flight behind the power curve

(a) recognise approach to minimum level flight speed during any phase of flight;

(b) resume normal balanced flight before entering flight behind the power curve;

(c) recover from flight behind the power curve at simulated low level in accordance with the height-velocity diagram.

2.10 AA3.10 – Execute forced landing from below 500 ft AGL

(a) identify potential forced-landing areas before and during low-level operations;

(b) recognise engine failure or any other emergency requiring a forced landing and execute recall actions;

(c) maintain control of gyroplane – select the most appropriate landing area within gliding distance while avoiding any powerlines or obstructions;

(d) manoeuvre gyroplane to a landing area that achieves the safest outcome;

(e) explain plan of action and landing techniques that would ensure the safest outcome when committed to forced landing on unfavourable terrain or water.

2.11 AA3.11 – Conduct operations over and under powerlines

(a) identify powerlines both in and outside the treatment area during an aerial survey;

(b) interpret powerline infrastructure cues so as to aid wire run identification;

(c) demonstrate technique for accurately assessing wire height, including flying parallel to wires;

(d) identify and manage other hazards relevant to operations near powerlines, such as pole stays, crop height, fences or machinery;

(e) make command decisions whether to fly over or under a wire;

(f) conduct treatment over wires, including adequate safety buffers for pull-up and let‑down and accurate cut-off and on of application equipment;

(g) conduct treatment under wires, including safe clearance;

(h) terminate approaches towards powerlines when passage beneath is unachievable;

(i) explain the relevant human factors that may affect operations near powerlines, particularly distraction, short-term memory limitations and inattentional blindness.

2.12 AA3.12 – Apply substances

(a) apply substances in accordance with aerial application management plan;

(b) establish and maintain correct application height relevant to terrain, application type and meteorological conditions;

(c) control airspeed and flight profile appropriately on entry/re-entry to treatment area;

(d) engage and shut off application equipment at appropriate points;

(e) manoeuvre around and over hazards in the treatment area with adequate safety buffers;

(f) use aircraft smoker (if fitted) to identify and monitor wind direction;

(g) monitor application flow rate, pressure and product remaining;

(h) conduct clean-up runs, including extra safety check for hazards;

(i) demonstrate command decisions to continue with, amend or suspend operations due to changing conditions.

2.13 AA3.13 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain

(a) manipulate gyroplane at low level in hilly terrain;

(b) establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type;

(c) demonstrate contour flying;

(d) identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness;

(e) demonstrate approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes;

(f) demonstrate turns in hilly terrain;

(g) demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects;

(h) demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows.

2.14 AA3.14 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations during low-level operations

(a) identify potential forced-landing areas before and during aerial application operations;

(b) identify abnormal or emergency situation;

(c) conduct abnormal or emergency procedures during application operations;

(d) maintain control of gyroplane, jettison load if required, and avoid any powerlines or hazards;

(e) conduct a practice forced landing from 500 ft.

2.15 AA3.15 – Jettison load (simulated where not fitted)

(a) jettison a full liquid load during take-off before lift off, and maintain control of gyroplane;

(b) jettison a full liquid load immediately after take-off and maintain control of gyroplane;

(c) jettison a full liquid load during flight and control pitch changes to ensure maintenance of altitude (+100/-0 ft) by adjustments of cyclic and power.

3 Range of variables

(a) activities are performed in accordance with published procedures;

(b) day VFR in variable weather conditions;

(c) approved aircraft;

(d) approved low-flying areas;

(e) operational airstrips;

(f) man-made or natural obstacles;

(g) undulating, hilly or mountainous terrain;

(h) emergency and abnormal situations;

(i) hazardous weather conditions;

(j) mental and physical fatigue;

(k) heat stress and dehydration;

(l) maintaining situational awareness;

(m) in-flight distractions.

4 Underpinning knowledge of the following:

(a) CASA exemptions relating to maximum take-off weight and applicability of other aircraft limitations;

(b) applicable regulations that relate to the conduct of a safe operation;

(c) low-level meteorology;

(d) relevant aerodynamics and aircraft performance;

(e) aircraft flight manual, performance, engine and systems;

(f) human factors;

(g) safety hazards and risks of flight at low level;

(h) role equipment;

(i) factors to be considered when determining payload weight for each application;

(j) aircraft configuration for the gyroplane being flown, when jettisoning a full load;

(k) characteristics of the gyroplane being flown when jettisoning a full load;

(l) flight control and throttle actions required to maintain control of the gyroplane being flown when jettisoning a full load.

AA4 Aeroplane firefighting operation

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct firefighting operations in aeroplanes.

Elements and performance criteria **AA4.1 – Applies human factors** demonstrates knowledge of and employs appropriate management strategies in response to human factors particularly relevant to fire operations, including: high workload; distraction and radios; dehydration; fatigue; CRM; time critical operational requirements; external factors. **AA4.2 – Pre-flight actions** conduct self-assessment fit for flight and planned operation; determine suitability of aircraft for type of operation; conduct a thorough pre-flight of aircraft and role equipment to determine serviceability for planned operations; check and correctly complete required maintenance documentation as applicable; confirm minimum equipment and minimum crew and instrumentation requirements for planned operations are met; apply TEM and risk management considerations, including human error; check safe operation of role equipment; confirm communication plan with fire agency and serviceability of communication equipment. **AA4.3 – Demonstrate understanding of generic fire agency procedures** demonstrate awareness of fire agency briefing processes; demonstrate awareness of fire agency incident control systems; able to explain the role and responsibilities of Air Attack Supervisor. **AA4.4 – Fire traffic management and other aircraft separation** demonstrate strong situational awareness of other aircraft and remotely piloted vehicles; demonstrate awareness of correct radio procedures and fire agency traffic management procedures; manage correct frequencies dependant on operational requirements. uses appropriate techniques and communication procedures when arriving at and departing from fire ground, refuelling site or replenishment points. **AA4.5 – Planning and risk management** determine the requirement to operate at low level, analyse the risk and implement a decision to safely conduct low-level operations; adequately identify potential hazards and operational requirements, assess risks and apply appropriate risk controls; demonstrate an ability to make a command decision on the safety or otherwise of the proposed application, including refusing to undertake an application where the risks are considered to be too high; demonstrates consideration of avoidance and escape techniques; determine the suitability of the current and forecast weather; make appropriate selection of application pattern and direction of treatment taking into consideration safety, efficiency, hazards and terrain; carefully plans fuel requirements; confirms acceptable aircraft performance for conditions; confirms location of ground support and firefighting personnel; confirms normal and abnormal ops communications and signals; confirms appropriate logistical considerations, including local airstrip condition, fuel, products, ground support and access to strip, SARWATCH, water, and personal supplies, including adequate water and food. **AA4.6 – Fly to, assess, land and take off from an operational airstrip** performs low-level navigation to an operational airstrip at an appropriate height; performs appropriate assessment of an operational airstrip, including strip length, conditions, direction, identification of hazards, meteorological conditions; selects the most suitable loading area, taking into account factors such as the safety of ground personnel and directions from the fire agency; consistently performs pre-landing and pre-take-off checks; selects a ‘no go, go around, commitment’ point for landings; selects a touchdown point for landings; identifies and manages issues relating to aircraft weight, performance, strip length, slope, surface, direction, load and meteorological conditions; demonstrates appropriate short-field landing and take-off techniques, including having her or his hand on the dump door handle for take-offs and being prepared to dump if required; identifies an appropriate dumping point for each take-off, including adequate safety buffers; demonstrates safe operations from a 1-way airstrip. **AA4.7 – Fly between operational airstrip and drop zone** performs low-level navigation from an operational airstrip to a drop zone; selects the most appropriate route and height between the operational strip and drop zone with considerations to terrain, stock, populated areas, housing and hazards. **AA4.8 – Conduct operations at a certified or registered aerodrome** performs operations in accordance with the requirements of published regulations. **AA4.9 – Conduct an aerial survey of a fire area** develops an appropriate and safe plan for conduct of an aerial survey; accurately identifies the fire area boundaries; confirms the map; identifies environmentally sensitive areas; identifies hazards on the map; checks and identifies any hazards not on the map, including fire specific hazards, sun glare and shadows from hills; accurately assesses wind speed and direction; confirms or appropriately amends the Application Management Plan, including pattern type and direction of treatment and possible suspension of application if conditions are not appropriate. **AA4.10 – Apply substances** safely and accurately apply substances in accordance with application management plan by doing the following: select the correct tank or door configuration and airspeed; make appropriate allowance for wind conditions; link application drops to create a continuous line of treatment; establish and maintain correct application height relevant to terrain, application type and meteorological conditions; control airspeed and flight profile appropriately on entry and re-entry to treatment area; engage and shut off application equipment at appropriate points; manoeuver around and over hazards in the treatment area with adequate safety buffers; demonstrate safe command decisions to continue with, amend or suspend operations due to changing conditions. **AA4.11 – Operate aircraft at maximum permissible weights for fire operations** determine take-off weight within legal requirements and relevant to strip length and conditions; operate safely and effectively at maximum weights during: taxi; take off and climb; approach and landing (including safe command decisions on dumping and strip selection); application; turns; obstacle avoidance. **AA4.12 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the aircraft at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows. **AA4.13 – Operate in high winds, high density altitude and high turbulence** demonstrate awareness of the principles of operating at low level in high winds, high density altitude and high turbulence; demonstrate sound judgement in assessing take-off conditions as being within the limitations of the aircraft. **AA4.14 – Low-visibility operations**

Able to explain low-visibility risks, including illusions such as false horizons and operating in smoke conditions.

**AA4.15 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations during low-level operations on a fire ground** identify potential forced-landing areas prior to and during firebombing operations; identify abnormal or emergency situation; conduct appropriate abnormal or emergency procedures; maintain control of aircraft, jettison load if required, and avoid any powerlines or hazards; successfully conduct a practice forced landing from 500 ft.

**AA4.16 – Jettison load from fire gate** jettison a full liquid load during take-off prior to lift off, and maintain control of the aircraft; jettison a full liquid load during flight and controls pitch changes to ensure maintenance of altitude by adjustments of elevator and power.

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR in variable weather conditions; approved aircraft; approved low-flying areas; airstrips; man-made or natural obstacles; undulating, hilly or mountainous terrain; emergency and abnormal situations; hazardous weather conditions and simulated fire conditions; mental and physical fatigue; heat stress and dehydration; maintaining situational awareness; in-flight distractions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: applicable regulations that relate to the conduct of a safe operation; low level and localised meteorology including the following: local meteorological conditions relevant to fire conditions; wind conditions likely to be found in fire conditions; wind conditions in hilly terrain, include lee winds; relevant aerodynamics and aircraft performance; aircraft flight manual, performance, engine and systems; relevant human factors; safety hazards and risks of flight at low level; pre-flight serviceability checks that are conducted on firefighting equipment that is fitted to the aircraft type being flown; conditions would indicate unserviceable firefighting equipment; role and authority of the Air Attack Supervisor and common fire agency procedures; radio frequencies being used by ground crews are obtained; factors that will determine the design and conduct of drop patterns; function and use of various fire suppressants and retardants; Reserved; the drop characteristics of suppressants and retardants with respect to drift; aircraft configuration for the aircraft being flown, when jettisoning a full load; flight characteristics of the aircraft being flown when jettisoning a full load; flight control and throttle actions required to maintain control of the aircraft being flown when jettisoning a full load; terminology used during fire-bombing operations including the following: head end of load; lead-in; roll up; tag-on; tail end of load; operational conditions under which fire-bombing could be suspended by an Air Attack Supervisor; environmental conditions under which an Air Attack Supervisor could suspend fire-firefighting operations; symptoms that could indicate aircrew fatigue; symptoms of dehydration and explain effects of dehydration on a pilot’s performance; container markings of fire retardant and suppression chemicals; toxicity conditions that apply to firefighting chemicals and the methods of avoiding any adverse effects; dispensing system, drop patters and emergency procedures; basic wildfires.

AA5 Helicopter firefighting operation

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct firefighting operations in helicopters.

Elements and performance criteria **AA5.1 – Applies human factors** demonstrate knowledge of and employ appropriate management strategies in response to human factors particularly relevant to fire operations, including: high workload; distraction and radios; dehydration; fatigue; CRM time critical operational requirements; external factors.. **AA5.2 – Pre-flight actions** conduct self-assessment fit for flight and planned operation; determine suitability of helicopter for type of operation; conduct a thorough pre-flight of helicopter and role equipment to determine serviceability for planned operations; check and correctly complete required maintenance documentation as applicable; confirm minimum equipment and minimum crew and instrumentation requirements for planned operations are met; apply TEM and risk management considerations, including human error; check safe operation of role equipment, including the serviceability of the jettison (dump) door if applicable or the sling jettison; confirm communication plan with fire agency and serviceability of communication equipment. **AA5.3 – Demonstrates understanding of generic fire agency procedures** demonstrates awareness of fire agency briefing processes; demonstrates awareness of fire agency incident control systems; able to explain the role and responsibilities of Air Attack Supervisor. **AA5.4 – Fire traffic management and other aircraft separation** demonstrates strong situational awareness of other aircraft and remotely piloted vehicles; demonstrates awareness of correct radio procedures and fire agency traffic management procedures; able to manage correct frequencies dependant on operational requirements; can explain appropriate techniques and communication procedures when arriving at and departing from fire ground, refuelling site or replenishment points. **AA5.5 – Planning and risk management** determine the requirement to operate at low level, analyse the risk and implement a decision to safely conduct low-level operations; adequately identify potential hazards and operational requirements, assess risks and apply appropriate risk controls; demonstrates consideration of avoidance and escape techniques; demonstrate an ability to make a command decision on the safety or otherwise of the proposed application, including refusing to undertake an application where the risks are considered to be too high; determine the suitability of the current and forecast weather; make appropriate selection of application pattern and direction of treatment taking into consideration safety, efficiency, hazards and terrain; carefully plans fuel requirements; confirms acceptable helicopter performance for conditions; confirms location of ground support and firefighting personnel; confirms normal and abnormal ops communications and signals; confirms appropriate logistical considerations, including local airstrip condition, fuel, products, ground support and access to strip, SARwatch, water, and personal supplies, including adequate water and food. **AA5.6 – Fly to, assess, land and take-off from an operational HLS or pick-up point** perform low-level navigation to an operational HLS or pick-up point at an appropriate safe height; perform appropriate assessment of an operational HLS or pick-up point, including dimensions, conditions, direction, identification of hazards, meteorological conditions; identify and manage issues relating to helicopter weight, performance, dimensions, load and meteorological conditions; consistently perform pre-landing and pre-take-off checks; demonstrate appropriate landing and take-off techniques; identify an appropriate dumping point for each take-off, including adequate safety buffers; demonstrate safe operations from a marginal HLS or pick-up point. **AA5.7 – Fly between operational HLS and drop zone** perform low-level navigation from an operational airstrip to a drop zone; selects the most appropriate route and height between the HLS or pick-up point and the drop zone with consideration to terrain, stock, populated areas, housing and hazards. **AA5.8 – Conduct operations at a certified or registered aerodrome**

Perform operations in accordance with the requirements of published regulations.

**AA5.9 – Conduct an aerial survey of a fire area** develops an appropriate and safe plan for conduct of an aerial survey; accurately identifies the fire area boundaries; confirms the map; identifies environmentally sensitive areas; identifies hazards on the map; identifies potential emergency landing area(s); checks and identifies any hazards not on the map, including fire specific hazards, sun glare and shadows from hills; accurately assesses wind speed and direction; confirms or appropriately amends the Application Management Plan, including pattern type and direction of treatment and possible suspension of application if conditions are not appropriate.

**AA5.10 – Apply substances** safely and accurately applies substances in accordance with application management plan by doing the following; select the correct tank or door configuration and airspeed; make appropriate allowance for wind conditions; link application drops to create a continuous line of treatment; perform a spot drops to achieve an accuracy of 80% of the substance falling vertically within a predetermined area; establishes and maintains correct application height relevant to terrain, application type and meteorological conditions; controls airspeed and flight profile appropriately on entry and re-entry to treatment area; engages and shuts off application equipment at appropriate points; manoeuvers around and over hazards in the treatment area with adequate safety buffers; demonstrates safe command decisions to continue with, amend or suspend operations due to changing conditions.

**AA5.11 – Reserved**

**AA5.12 – Replenish helicopter load with snorkel or bucket** demonstrates safe identification and assessment of replenishment site, including consideration of entry and exit direction, hazards, surrounding terrain, emergency actions, wind conditions and impact of heavier load on exit performance; demonstrates safe speed control and height loss on approach to target replenishment spot (e.g. dam); accurately places bucket or snorkel into water; maintains safe hover while taking on load, smoothly adjusting for increasing weight; demonstrates safe technique in lifting bucket or snorkel smoothly and maintaining safe hover and exit under new load; maintains safe control of the helicopter and demonstrates safe command decisions to jettison or replace bucket into water if helicopter is unable to safely lift load.

**AA5.13 – Operate helicopter at maximum permissible weights for fire operations** determines take-off weight within legal requirements and relevant to HLS dimensions and conditions; operates safely and effectively at maximum weights during: taxi; take off and climb; approach and landing, including safe command decisions on dumping and HLS selection; application; turns; obstacle avoidance.

**AA5.14 – Manage known helicopter risks during firefighting operations** demonstrate sound decision making in assessing likely hover performance considering load, density altitude, ground surface and relative wind; demonstrates awareness of and correct techniques in managing rotor disc behaviour under reduced or negative ‘g ‘; demonstrate awareness of and correct techniques in avoiding dynamic rollover; demonstrate awareness of and correct techniques in avoiding loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE) and vortex ring state.

**AA5.15 – Low-visibility operations**

Able to explain low-visibility risks, including illusions such as false horizons and operating in smoke conditions.

**AA5.16 – Operate at low level in hilly terrain** safely manipulate the helicopter at low level in hilly terrain; establish and maintain safe height relevant to application type; demonstrate safe contour flying; identify and select appropriate natural markers to aid situational awareness; demonstrate safe approaches to higher ground, including identification of escape routes; demonstrate safe turns in hilly terrain; demonstrate awareness and management of the effects of wind and turbulence in hilly terrain, including lee effects; demonstrate awareness of illusions in hilly terrain, including false horizon effect and shadows.

**AA5.17 – Operate in high winds, high density altitude and high turbulence** demonstrate awareness of the principles of operating at low level in high winds, high density altitude and high turbulence; demonstrate sound judgement in assessing take-off conditions as being within the limitations of the helicopter.;

**AA5.18 – Manage abnormal and emergency situations during low-level operations on a fire ground** identify potential forced-landing areas prior to and during firebombing operations; identify abnormal or emergency situation; conduct appropriate abnormal or emergency procedures; maintain control of helicopter including adequate coordination of collective, jettison load if required, and avoid any powerlines or hazards; successfully conduct a practice forced landing from 500 ft.

**AA5.19 – Jettison load from fire gate** jettison a full liquid load at take-off, and maintains control of the helicopter; jettison a full liquid load during flight and ensures maintenance of altitude (+100 -0 ft).

Range of variables activities are performed in accordance with published procedures; day VFR in variable weather conditions; approved helicopter; approved low-flying areas; operational HLSs and pick-up points; man-made or natural obstacles; undulating, hilly or mountainous terrain; emergency and abnormal situations; hazardous weather conditions and simulated fire conditions; mental and physical fatigue; heat stress and dehydration; maintaining situational awareness; in-flight distractions.

Underpinning knowledge of the following: applicable regulations that relate to the conduct of a safe operation; low level and localised meteorology: local meteorological conditions relevant to fire conditions; wind conditions likely to be found in fire conditions; wind conditions in hilly terrain, including lee winds; relevant aerodynamics and helicopter performance; helicopter flight manual, performance, engine and systems; human factors; safety hazards and risks of flight at low level; pre-flight serviceability checks that are conducted on fire-firefighting equipment that is fitted to the helicopter type being flown; conditions would indicate unserviceable fire-firefighting equipment; role and authority of the Air Attack Supervisor and common fire agency procedures; radio frequencies being used by ground crews are obtained; factors that will determine the design and conduct of drop patterns; function and use of various fire suppressants and retardants; Reserved; drop characteristics of suppressants and retardants with respect to drift; helicopter configuration for the helicopter being flown, when jettisoning a full load; flight characteristics of the helicopter being flown when jettisoning a full load; flight control and throttle actions required to maintain control of the helicopter being flown when jettisoning a full load; terminology used during fire-bombing operations: head end of load; lead-in; roll up; tag-on; tail end of load; operational conditions under which fire-bombing could be suspended by an Air Attack Supervisor; environmental conditions under which an Air Attack Supervisor could suspend fire-bombing operations; symptoms that could indicate aircrew fatigue; symptoms of dehydration and explain effects of dehydration on a pilot’s performance; markings of fire retardant and suppression chemicals; toxicity conditions that apply to firefighting chemicals and the methods of avoiding any adverse effects; dispensing system, drop patters and emergency procedures; basic wildfires.

AA6 Night aerial application operation

Unit description

This unit describes the skills and knowledge required to conduct an aerial application operation other than a firefighting operation at night.

Elements and performance criteria **AA6.1 – Aircraft and equipment serviceability** confirm all required aircraft lighting is installed and serviceable; confirm additional instrumentation required for night flying is installed and serviceable. **AA6.2 – Conduct risk assessment of operation**

Demonstrate an ability to assess forecast meteorological conditions for night operations, including moon state and to make a command decision (i.e. go-no go) based on her or his safety assessment.

**AA6.3 – Pre-flight actions** thorough risk assessment of planned treatment are conducted during daylight; conduct self-assessment fit for night flying.

**AA6.4 – Determine whether an airstrip or HLS is suitable for night operations** determine whether airstrip or /HLS dimensions and lighting is suitable and available for night operations; identify potential obstacles surrounding the airstrip or HLS and in the runway end splays.
